levels.title: Energy comparison

levels.component_tex:
Write $q=n/d$ and $\sigma=s/h$, and work throughout with $2a\le s\le3$. Take $0<\gamma<w_0/8$ initially. Constants in the wall estimates can be taken independent of $\gamma$. Prefactors in the interior estimates may depend on $\gamma$. A power $\sigma^m$ below denotes a fixed power, which can be increased finitely many times. The inverse auxiliary chart
\[
Y=\frac{\sqrt2\tau+aQ}{1+W\cdot W/2},\qquad P=WY,\qquad Z=\sqrt2Y-\tau
\]
fixes the shape of the fiber in $(W,Q)$ and gives $y\asymp s$. Where the wall $r=0$ meets the support of the cutoff, $|Q|\le1/20$ forces $|W|\ge\sqrt3w_0/2$. We use a separate interior region with $|W|\le\gamma$ and $|Q|\le1/400$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textit{Spatial average and upper bounds on the current.}
For a fixed dimensional constant $D\ge1$ to be chosen, set $P_*(X)=(J_{Ds}*|g_T|^2)^{1/d}$ and $M=2n+4$. The kernel $J_{Ds}$ is strictly positive and $\|g_T\|_2=1$, so $P_*>0$. Termwise differentiation of the periodized kernel through order two gives $|\nabla_X^j J_{Ds}|\le C(Ds)^{-j}J_{Ds}$, since the rescaled Euclidean kernel has the same relative derivative bounds. Differentiating the $d$th root and using the order-one estimate for its quadratic term gives
\[
|\nabla_X^j P_*|\le C(Ds)^{-j}P_*\quad(j=1,2),\qquad
\int_{\mathbb T^n}P_*^{d+1}\,\mathrm dX\le\|g_T\|_{p_c}^{p_c}.
\]
The last inequality is Young's inequality in $L^q$ for the probability kernel, using $d+1=n$ and $2q=p_c$.

By Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-2-2}, the entries of the column whose outer product is $A^0$ are sums of scalar multiplier outputs placed in quaternionic slots, with scalar symbols a bounded smooth factor times
\[
(\kappa/y)^{d/2}e^{-\Psi},\qquad \Psi=\kappa y|W-v|^2/2.
\]
Multiply the symbols by a fixed smooth annular cutoff equal to one on the data and supported where $|v|<w_0/3$ and $\kappa>0$. In the scaled frequency variable $\eta=h\xi$, the derivatives of the symbols through order $M$ are bounded by $C(hs)^{-d/2}\sigma^m$. Indeed, $h\kappa$ and $v$ are smooth on this cutoff with uniformly bounded derivatives and $h\kappa$ is bounded away from zero. Every derivative of $\Psi$ through order $M$ costs at most $C\sigma$. Where $r=0$ and $g(Q)\ne0$, one has $|W-v|\ge\sqrt3w_0/2-w_0/3>0$ on this enlarged cap. There the derivative bound gains a factor $e^{-c_0\sigma}$, with $c_0>0$ independent of $\gamma$.

If $B$ bounds the derivatives through order $M$ of a symbol supported in the fixed scaled annulus, apply $(1-\Delta_\eta)^{n+2}$ to the symbol in the inverse Fourier integral. Its absolute Euclidean kernel is at most $CBh^{-n}(1+|X/h|^2)^{-M/2}$. Periodizing gives an absolute kernel bound by $CBJ_h$ on the torus; the same argument works in a rotated frame and its rotated lattice. By Cauchy--Schwarz against the probability kernel, the squared modulus of the output is bounded by $CB^2(J_h*|g_T|^2)$. This applies to each of the finitely many scalar slots from the current. The smoothing of $A^0$ applies one more convolution by $J_h$. On $\mathbb R^n$, either $|Y'|\ge |X|/2$ or $|X-Y'|\ge |X|/2$ in the convolution variable $Y'$, so the convolution of two copies of the positive Euclidean kernel is bounded by a constant times the kernel itself. Periodization gives $J_h*J_h\le CJ_h$. Since $Ds\ge h$, comparison term by term gives $J_h\le(Ds/h)^nJ_{Ds}$. Using $(hs)^{-d}=s^{-2d}\sigma^d$ and relabeling $m,c_0$ gives the operator norm estimates
\[
\|A_{\mathrm w}\|\le Cs^{-2d}\sigma^mP_*^d\quad(r\le0),\qquad
\|A_{\mathrm w}\|\le Cs^{-2d}\sigma^m e^{-c_0\sigma}P_*^d\quad(r=0).
\]

The time cofactor of $H(r)$ is $\det H_{\mathrm{fib}}(r)$ by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2}; by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1} this is comparable to $a^{-2}s^{-2d}$. A nearest lattice term in $J_{Ds}$ gives the lower bound $\inf J_{Ds}\ge c_D h^{M-n}$: the nearest representative is in a fixed bounded set, $h\le s\le3$, and the scaled kernel there is bounded below by $c_Ds^{M-n}$. Thus $P_*^d\ge c_Dh^{M-n}$. As $a\ge h$ and $50n-2\ge M-n$, this absorbs the contribution $Ch^{50n}a^{-2}s^{-2d}$ of the cofactor in the density; in particular
\[
\mu\le Cs^{-2d}\sigma^mP_*^d\quad(r\le0).
\]
We also use the weaker ceiling $\mu^{1/d}\le\lambda$ for small enough $h$ uniformly on the fibers. By Lemma~\ref{ms:wave-cap-estimates}, $\kappa\asymp h^{-1}$ and the amplitudes sum in absolute value to $O(h^{-n/2})$. Each wave weight is $O(h^{-d})$ since $y\asymp s\ge h$, and each column factor is bounded. Hence $\|(A^0)\|\lesssim h^{-n-2d}$; smoothing, cutting off and adding the preceding cofactor bound give $\mu\lesssim h^{-n-2d}+h^{50n-2-2d}$. This is at most $h^{-30nd}=\lambda^d$ for sufficiently small $h$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textit{The wall comparison and the flux.}
Put $R=H_{\mathrm{fib}}(r)$ and $B_{\mathrm{fib}}=H_{\mathrm{fib}}(B_0)$. Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1} gives $R\ge cs^{-2}I$ and $G_{\mathrm{fib}}(r)G_{\mathrm{fib}}(r)^*\le CR$. The Hessian product rule of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-1} shows that $H_{\mathrm{fib}}(rP_*)$ is the sum of $P_*R$, $rH_{\mathrm{fib}}(P_*)$, and the two mixed gradient products. Against a quaternionic vector $e$, the pairings of $G_{\mathrm{fib}}(r)$ and $G_{\mathrm{fib}}(P_*)$ with $e$ are bounded in modulus by $C(e^*Re)^{1/2}$ and $CD^{-1}P_*(e^*Re)^{1/2}$, respectively. The second derivatives of $P_*$ and $|r|\le1$ bound the cost of $rH_{\mathrm{fib}}(P_*)$ by $CD^{-2}P_*R$ in quadratic form. Hence $H_{\mathrm{fib}}(rP_*)\ge(1-C/D)P_*R$; fix $D$ large so the coefficient is at least $1/2$.

The regularizer gives $\mu>0$ by the positivity of $R$ and of $A_{\mathrm w}$. The background $B_{\mathrm{fib}}$ has rank one and positive eigenvalue comparable to $\lambda$ by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1}. The Dirichlet theorem and comparison of Theorem~\ref{ms:thm-a-1} apply because $r$ has strictly positive fiber Hessian, $\det B_{\mathrm{fib}}=0$, and the prescribed determinant is $\lambda\mu>0$. In particular the smooth $u$ exists and $u\le0$. For $v_*=C_1\sigma^{m_1}rP_*$, compare its positive definite Hessian plus the background to $B_{\mathrm{fib}}+\tfrac12 c C_1\sigma^{m_1}P_*s^{-2}I$. By determinant monotonicity from Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2} and the background eigenvalue bound this gives
\[
\det(B_{\mathrm{fib}}+H_{\mathrm{fib}}(v_*))
\ge c\lambda(C_1\sigma^{m_1}P_*s^{-2})^d\ge\lambda\mu
\]
for $m_1,C_1$ large enough. Since the two potentials have the same zero boundary values, comparison gives $v_*\le u\le0$. Dividing by $r<0$ and extending smoothly to the boundary as in Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-4-2} gives $0\le u/r\le C_1\sigma^{m_1}P_*$.

Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-4-2} gives smoothness of $\mathcal F$ in the entire open parameter domain: the Dirichlet solution is smooth up to the moving wall and the auxiliary chart identifies the fibers with a fixed domain. The determinant in the segment integral is polynomial, so it remains smooth at $\theta=0$. Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-3}, applied on each fiber with the density $\mu=A_{TT}$ and its smooth Dirichlet solution $u$, gives
\[
 0\le \frac{n-1}{n+1}\int_{\Omega_z}(-u)\mu\,\mathrm d\zeta
 \le \mathcal F(z)\le \int_{\Omega_z}(-u)\mu\,\mathrm d\zeta .
\]
Here $u\le0$ and $\mu>0$ follow from the Dirichlet construction on each fiber. The volume comparison of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1} gives an auxiliary volume $O(a^2s^{2d})$. Using the upper bounds on $u/r$ and $\mu$ and $\int P_*^{d+1}\,\mathrm dX\le\|g_T\|_{p_c}^{p_c}$, we obtain
\[
\mathcal F(T,\tau)\le Ca^2\sigma^m\|g_T\|_{p_c}^{p_c}.
\]

For the wall flux, Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-2-2} gives $(\partial\Phi)A^0=0$. By the gradient identity in Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-1}, the Hermitian current kills $G(|\Phi|^2)$, and this survives multiplication by $g(Q)$ and convolution because $\partial\Phi$ is independent of $X$. Hence only the $|W|^2/w_0^2$ part of the full $G(r)$ contributes. Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1} gives $|G(|W|^2)|\lesssim s^{-1}$, so $G(r)^*A_{\mathrm w}G(r)\le Cs^{-2}\|A_{\mathrm w}\|$. In the $(W,Q)$ chart the coarea measure $\delta(r)\,\mathrm dP\,\mathrm dZ$ has total mass at most $Ca^2s^{2d}$ by the same volume comparison and coarea on the fixed ellipsoid. Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-4-2} bounds $\Delta_z\mathcal F$ above by the wall integral of $(u/r)G(r)^*A_{\mathrm w}G(r)\delta(r)$. The wall current bound and the upper bound for $u/r$ then yield
\[
\Delta_z\mathcal F(T,\tau)\le C(a/s)^2\sigma^me^{-c_0\sigma}\|g_T\|_{p_c}^{p_c}.
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textit{Interior recovery and lower bound.}
Take a center $(X,P,Z)$ with $|W|\le\gamma$, $|Q|\le1/400$. The radius-$h$ ball in the $3n$ real spatial slots about the center fits inside $|W|\le2\gamma$, $|Q|\le1/100$ for sufficiently large $K\gamma$ and $K$: the chart bounds $\nabla W=O(s^{-1})$, $\nabla\Phi=O(1)$ and gives changes at most $Ch/s$ and $Ch$ along such segments. These derivative bounds hold up to the edge of the enlarged patch, so a first exit would violate the chosen bounds. The cutoff is identically one on this ball.

By the time-component identity in Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-2-2}, $|\mathsf S_0g_T|^2\le A^0_{TT}$. Multiply the reciprocal of this symbol from Lemma~\ref{ms:wave-cap-estimates} by a smooth annular cutoff equal to one on the data, supported where $|v|\le2\gamma$. On the ball $|W|\le2\gamma$, so $|W-v|\le4\gamma$ on this enlarged cap, and $\Psi\le C\gamma^2\sigma$. The derivatives through order $M$ in $\eta=h\xi$ are bounded by
\[
B_{\mathrm{inv}}=C_\gamma(hs)^{d/2}\sigma^me^{C\gamma^2\sigma}.
\]
This follows by differentiation since $h\kappa$ stays bounded away from zero and all derivatives of $\Psi$ cost at most $C\sigma$. Derivatives of the small cap cutoff affect $C_\gamma$, while the constant $C$ in the exponential is independent of $\gamma$.

Apply the kernel estimate and Cauchy--Schwarz to this inverse acting on $\mathsf S_0g_T$. At the real center $X$ and any auxiliary point in the ball it gives
\[
|g_T(X)|^2\le CB_{\mathrm{inv}}^2(J_h*A^0_{TT})(X).
\]
If $|X'-X|\le h$, the two kernel values $J_h(X'-Y')$ and $J_h(X-Y')$ are uniformly comparable, by the analogous termwise statement for the Euclidean kernel. Since $\mu\ge J_h*A^0_{TT}$ where $g(Q)=1$, this proves the pointwise lower bound on the entire ball
\[
\mu\ge m_X:=c_\gamma(hs)^{-d}\sigma^{-m}e^{-C_2\gamma^2\sigma}|g_T(X)|^2.
\]

Let $\ell$ be the Euclidean distance to the center in the spatial slots. When $m_X>0$, the quadratic $v_b=\epsilon m_X^{1/d}(\ell^2-h^2)$ has zero ball-boundary value and fiber Hessian $6\epsilon m_X^{1/d}I$ by the three-slot Hessian formula. The rank-one background and $m_X^{1/d}\le \mu^{1/d}\le\lambda$ give, for a fixed small $\epsilon>0$,
\[
\det(B_{\mathrm{fib}}+H_{\mathrm{fib}}(v_b))
\le C[(\epsilon m_X^{1/d})^n+\lambda(\epsilon m_X^{1/d})^d]
\le\lambda m_X .
\]
Both Hessians are positive definite. Since $u\le0=v_b$ on the ball boundary and $\det D_u=\lambda\mu\ge\lambda m_X$, the local comparison in Theorem~\ref{ms:thm-a-1} gives $u\le v_b$ on the ball. At the center, $(-u)\mu\ge\epsilon h^2m_X^{1+1/d}$; if $m_X=0$ this follows from $u\le0$ and $\mu\ge0$.

The auxiliary volume of the centers in $(P,Z)$ is comparable to $a^2s^{2d}\gamma^{2d}$ by the Jacobian in Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1}. Since $1+1/d=q$ and $2q=p_c$, integration over the centers, followed by the lower comparison in Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-3}, gives
\[
\mathcal F(T,\tau)\ge c_\gamma a^2\sigma^{-m}e^{-C_3\gamma^2\sigma}\|g_T\|_{p_c}^{p_c};
\]
here $h^2s^{2d}(hs)^{-dq}=\sigma^{n-2}$ and the constant in the exponential remains independent of $\gamma$.

Now fix $\gamma$ so that $C_3\gamma^2<c_0/2$. Choose $K$ large enough for the ball inclusions and so that $h<1/(4K)$ gives the density ceiling used above. The interior bound is positive since $\|g_T\|_2=1$. Dividing the flux estimate by it gives $C_\gamma s^{-2}\sigma^{2m}e^{-(c_0-C_3\gamma^2)\sigma}$, bounded by $Cs^{-2}e^{-c\sigma}$ after decreasing the exponential constant. At $s=4a$ and $s=2a$ the ratios $\sigma$ are respectively $4K$ and $2K$. The energy upper bound at the first radius with $g_0=f$ and the lower bound at the second radius give the stated circle estimates.
levels.section_title: Energy estimates on a fixed fiber: Proof of Proposition prop-5-1
levels.statement:
Let $n\ge2$, $d=n-1$, $p_c=2n/d$, and fix $0<c_1<c_2$. On the spatial torus $\mathbb T^n=\mathbb R^n/(100\mathbb Z)^n$ write $X=(x,b)$ in an orthonormal frame with $x\in\mathbb R^d$. For each frequency with $\xi_b+|\xi|>0$ put $\kappa=(\xi_b+|\xi|)/\sqrt2$ and $v=\xi_x/\kappa$. There are constants $\gamma>0$, $K\ge1$, and $c,C>0$, depending only on $n,c_1,c_2$, with the following property. Let $0<h<1/(4K)$, $a=Kh$, and let $f$ be a trigonometric polynomial of $L^2$ norm one whose Fourier support consists of frequencies with $c_1\le h|\xi|\le c_2$, $\xi_b+|\xi|>0$, and $|v|\le\gamma$. Write $g_T=e^{-\mathrm i T|D|}f$.

Here is the energy used in the conclusion. For $z=(T,\tau)$, where $\tau$ lies in the quaternionic complex plane $\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}$ and $s=|\tau|\in(a,4)$, the auxiliary spatial coordinates are $(P,Z)\in\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}^{d}\times\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}$. Set
\[
Y=(\tau+Z)/\sqrt2,\quad S_1=(Z-\tau)/\sqrt2,\quad
y=|Y|,\quad W=P/Y,\quad \Phi=S_1+P\cdot P/(2Y),\quad Q=\Phi/a .
\]
Dots between complex vectors are bilinear. Take $w_0=1/10$ and let $\Omega_z$ be the torus times the auxiliary domain $Y\ne0$, $r=|W|^2/w_0^2+100|Q|^2-1<0$. Write $\mathrm d\zeta=\mathrm dX\,\mathrm dP\,\mathrm dZ$. The full quaternionic Hessian and gradient $H,G$ use the three real slots $(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j)$ for each index, where $\mathbf k\mathbf i=\mathbf j$. In these slots with basis $e_\alpha$, their entries are
\[
H_{ab}(w)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta=0}^2 e_\alpha\overline{e_\beta}\,\partial_{a\alpha}\partial_{b\beta}w,\qquad
G_a(w)=\sum_{\alpha=0}^2e_\alpha\partial_{a\alpha}w .
\]
A subscript $\mathrm{fib}$ takes the spatial block at fixed $z$. Determinants and cofactors of these Hermitian matrices are the Moore determinant and its matrix derivative, respectively.

For $\ell>0$ let $J_\ell$ be the periodization of $c_n\ell^{-n}(1+|X/\ell|^2)^{-n-2}$, with $c_n$ chosen so the kernel integrates to one. Let $0\le g\le1$ be a fixed smooth cutoff equal to one on $|Q|\le1/100$ and zero on $|Q|\ge1/20$. The wave current $A^0=\chi\chi^*$ in null coordinates is given by
\[
\chi=\sum_\xi
\begin{pmatrix}1\\(v+W)/2\\-W\cdot v/2\end{pmatrix}
\iota_{Y/y}(\overline{\widehat f(\xi)e^{\mathrm i(X\cdot\xi-T|\xi|)}})
(\kappa/y)^{d/2}e^{-\kappa y|W-v|^2/2},
\qquad
\iota_e(\alpha+\mathrm i\beta)=\alpha+e\mathbf i\beta .
\]
Return to physical coordinates by $T=(t-s_0)/\sqrt2$, $b=(t+s_0)/\sqrt2$ in the coordinate index. With convolution in $X$, put
\[
A_{\mathrm w}=g(Q)(J_h*A^0),\qquad
\mu=(A_{\mathrm w})_{TT}+h^{50n}\operatorname{Cof}(H(r))_{TT},\qquad
B_0=\lambda|\Phi|^2,\quad \lambda=h^{-30n},\quad
D_w=H_{\mathrm{fib}}(B_0+w).
\]
For the smooth zero-boundary solution $u$ of $D_u>0$, $\det D_u=\lambda\mu$ on the fiber, set
\[
\mathcal F(T,\tau)=\int_{\Omega_z}(-u)\mu\,\mathrm d\zeta+
\frac1\lambda\int_{\Omega_z}u\left(\int_0^1\det D_{\theta u}\,\mathrm d\theta\right)\mathrm d\zeta .
\]
The energy $\mathcal F$ is nonnegative and smooth on the open parameter domain $\mathbb R_T\times\{\tau:a<|\tau|<4\}$. With all norms on the torus,
\begin{align*}
\mathcal F(0,\tau)&\le Ca^2\|f\|_{p_c}^{p_c} && (|\tau|=4a),\\
\mathcal F(T,\tau)&\ge ca^2\|g_T\|_{p_c}^{p_c} && (|\tau|=2a),\\
\Delta_z\mathcal F(T,\tau)&\le Cs^{-2}e^{-cs/h}\mathcal F(T,\tau) && (2a\le s\le3).
\end{align*}
The last two estimates hold for all real $T$, and $\Delta_z$ is the Euclidean Laplacian in $T$ and the two real coordinates of $\tau$.
levels.text:
Write $q=n/d$ and $\sigma=s/h$, and work throughout with $2a\le s\le3$. Take $0<\gamma<w_0/8$ initially. Constants in the wall estimates can be taken independent of $\gamma$. Prefactors in the interior estimates may depend on $\gamma$. A power $\sigma^m$ below denotes a fixed power, which can be increased finitely many times. The inverse auxiliary chart
\[
Y=\frac{\sqrt2\tau+aQ}{1+W\cdot W/2},\qquad P=WY,\qquad Z=\sqrt2Y-\tau
\]
fixes the shape of the fiber in $(W,Q)$ and gives $y\asymp s$. Where the wall $r=0$ meets the support of the cutoff, $|Q|\le1/20$ forces $|W|\ge\sqrt3w_0/2$. We use a separate interior region with $|W|\le\gamma$ and $|Q|\le1/400$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textit{Spatial average and upper bounds on the current.}
For a fixed dimensional constant $D\ge1$ to be chosen, set $P_*(X)=(J_{Ds}*|g_T|^2)^{1/d}$ and $M=2n+4$. The kernel $J_{Ds}$ is strictly positive and $\|g_T\|_2=1$, so $P_*>0$. Termwise differentiation of the periodized kernel through order two gives $|\nabla_X^j J_{Ds}|\le C(Ds)^{-j}J_{Ds}$, since the rescaled Euclidean kernel has the same relative derivative bounds. Differentiating the $d$th root and using the order-one estimate for its quadratic term gives
\[
|\nabla_X^j P_*|\le C(Ds)^{-j}P_*\quad(j=1,2),\qquad
\int_{\mathbb T^n}P_*^{d+1}\,\mathrm dX\le\|g_T\|_{p_c}^{p_c}.
\]
The last inequality is Young's inequality in $L^q$ for the probability kernel, using $d+1=n$ and $2q=p_c$.

By Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-2-2}, the entries of the column whose outer product is $A^0$ are sums of scalar multiplier outputs placed in quaternionic slots, with scalar symbols a bounded smooth factor times
\[
(\kappa/y)^{d/2}e^{-\Psi},\qquad \Psi=\kappa y|W-v|^2/2.
\]
Multiply the symbols by a fixed smooth annular cutoff equal to one on the data and supported where $|v|<w_0/3$ and $\kappa>0$. In the scaled frequency variable $\eta=h\xi$, the derivatives of the symbols through order $M$ are bounded by $C(hs)^{-d/2}\sigma^m$. Indeed, $h\kappa$ and $v$ are smooth on this cutoff with uniformly bounded derivatives and $h\kappa$ is bounded away from zero. Every derivative of $\Psi$ through order $M$ costs at most $C\sigma$. Where $r=0$ and $g(Q)\ne0$, one has $|W-v|\ge\sqrt3w_0/2-w_0/3>0$ on this enlarged cap. There the derivative bound gains a factor $e^{-c_0\sigma}$, with $c_0>0$ independent of $\gamma$.

If $B$ bounds the derivatives through order $M$ of a symbol supported in the fixed scaled annulus, apply $(1-\Delta_\eta)^{n+2}$ to the symbol in the inverse Fourier integral. Its absolute Euclidean kernel is at most $CBh^{-n}(1+|X/h|^2)^{-M/2}$. Periodizing gives an absolute kernel bound by $CBJ_h$ on the torus; the same argument works in a rotated frame and its rotated lattice. By Cauchy--Schwarz against the probability kernel, the squared modulus of the output is bounded by $CB^2(J_h*|g_T|^2)$. This applies to each of the finitely many scalar slots from the current. The smoothing of $A^0$ applies one more convolution by $J_h$. On $\mathbb R^n$, either $|Y'|\ge |X|/2$ or $|X-Y'|\ge |X|/2$ in the convolution variable $Y'$, so the convolution of two copies of the positive Euclidean kernel is bounded by a constant times the kernel itself. Periodization gives $J_h*J_h\le CJ_h$. Since $Ds\ge h$, comparison term by term gives $J_h\le(Ds/h)^nJ_{Ds}$. Using $(hs)^{-d}=s^{-2d}\sigma^d$ and relabeling $m,c_0$ gives the operator norm estimates
\[
\|A_{\mathrm w}\|\le Cs^{-2d}\sigma^mP_*^d\quad(r\le0),\qquad
\|A_{\mathrm w}\|\le Cs^{-2d}\sigma^m e^{-c_0\sigma}P_*^d\quad(r=0).
\]

The time cofactor of $H(r)$ is $\det H_{\mathrm{fib}}(r)$ by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2}; by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1} this is comparable to $a^{-2}s^{-2d}$. A nearest lattice term in $J_{Ds}$ gives the lower bound $\inf J_{Ds}\ge c_D h^{M-n}$: the nearest representative is in a fixed bounded set, $h\le s\le3$, and the scaled kernel there is bounded below by $c_Ds^{M-n}$. Thus $P_*^d\ge c_Dh^{M-n}$. As $a\ge h$ and $50n-2\ge M-n$, this absorbs the contribution $Ch^{50n}a^{-2}s^{-2d}$ of the cofactor in the density; in particular
\[
\mu\le Cs^{-2d}\sigma^mP_*^d\quad(r\le0).
\]
We also use the weaker ceiling $\mu^{1/d}\le\lambda$ for small enough $h$ uniformly on the fibers. By Lemma~\ref{ms:wave-cap-estimates}, $\kappa\asymp h^{-1}$ and the amplitudes sum in absolute value to $O(h^{-n/2})$. Each wave weight is $O(h^{-d})$ since $y\asymp s\ge h$, and each column factor is bounded. Hence $\|(A^0)\|\lesssim h^{-n-2d}$; smoothing, cutting off and adding the preceding cofactor bound give $\mu\lesssim h^{-n-2d}+h^{50n-2-2d}$. This is at most $h^{-30nd}=\lambda^d$ for sufficiently small $h$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textit{The wall comparison and the flux.}
Put $R=H_{\mathrm{fib}}(r)$ and $B_{\mathrm{fib}}=H_{\mathrm{fib}}(B_0)$. Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1} gives $R\ge cs^{-2}I$ and $G_{\mathrm{fib}}(r)G_{\mathrm{fib}}(r)^*\le CR$. The Hessian product rule of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-1} shows that $H_{\mathrm{fib}}(rP_*)$ is the sum of $P_*R$, $rH_{\mathrm{fib}}(P_*)$, and the two mixed gradient products. Against a quaternionic vector $e$, the pairings of $G_{\mathrm{fib}}(r)$ and $G_{\mathrm{fib}}(P_*)$ with $e$ are bounded in modulus by $C(e^*Re)^{1/2}$ and $CD^{-1}P_*(e^*Re)^{1/2}$, respectively. The second derivatives of $P_*$ and $|r|\le1$ bound the cost of $rH_{\mathrm{fib}}(P_*)$ by $CD^{-2}P_*R$ in quadratic form. Hence $H_{\mathrm{fib}}(rP_*)\ge(1-C/D)P_*R$; fix $D$ large so the coefficient is at least $1/2$.

The regularizer gives $\mu>0$ by the positivity of $R$ and of $A_{\mathrm w}$. The background $B_{\mathrm{fib}}$ has rank one and positive eigenvalue comparable to $\lambda$ by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1}. The Dirichlet theorem and comparison of Theorem~\ref{ms:thm-a-1} apply because $r$ has strictly positive fiber Hessian, $\det B_{\mathrm{fib}}=0$, and the prescribed determinant is $\lambda\mu>0$. In particular the smooth $u$ exists and $u\le0$. For $v_*=C_1\sigma^{m_1}rP_*$, compare its positive definite Hessian plus the background to $B_{\mathrm{fib}}+\tfrac12 c C_1\sigma^{m_1}P_*s^{-2}I$. By determinant monotonicity from Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2} and the background eigenvalue bound this gives
\[
\det(B_{\mathrm{fib}}+H_{\mathrm{fib}}(v_*))
\ge c\lambda(C_1\sigma^{m_1}P_*s^{-2})^d\ge\lambda\mu
\]
for $m_1,C_1$ large enough. Since the two potentials have the same zero boundary values, comparison gives $v_*\le u\le0$. Dividing by $r<0$ and extending smoothly to the boundary as in Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-4-2} gives $0\le u/r\le C_1\sigma^{m_1}P_*$.

Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-4-2} gives smoothness of $\mathcal F$ in the entire open parameter domain: the Dirichlet solution is smooth up to the moving wall and the auxiliary chart identifies the fibers with a fixed domain. The determinant in the segment integral is polynomial, so it remains smooth at $\theta=0$. Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-3}, applied on each fiber with the density $\mu=A_{TT}$ and its smooth Dirichlet solution $u$, gives
\[
 0\le \frac{n-1}{n+1}\int_{\Omega_z}(-u)\mu\,\mathrm d\zeta
 \le \mathcal F(z)\le \int_{\Omega_z}(-u)\mu\,\mathrm d\zeta .
\]
Here $u\le0$ and $\mu>0$ follow from the Dirichlet construction on each fiber. The volume comparison of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1} gives an auxiliary volume $O(a^2s^{2d})$. Using the upper bounds on $u/r$ and $\mu$ and $\int P_*^{d+1}\,\mathrm dX\le\|g_T\|_{p_c}^{p_c}$, we obtain
\[
\mathcal F(T,\tau)\le Ca^2\sigma^m\|g_T\|_{p_c}^{p_c}.
\]

For the wall flux, Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-2-2} gives $(\partial\Phi)A^0=0$. By the gradient identity in Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-1}, the Hermitian current kills $G(|\Phi|^2)$, and this survives multiplication by $g(Q)$ and convolution because $\partial\Phi$ is independent of $X$. Hence only the $|W|^2/w_0^2$ part of the full $G(r)$ contributes. Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1} gives $|G(|W|^2)|\lesssim s^{-1}$, so $G(r)^*A_{\mathrm w}G(r)\le Cs^{-2}\|A_{\mathrm w}\|$. In the $(W,Q)$ chart the coarea measure $\delta(r)\,\mathrm dP\,\mathrm dZ$ has total mass at most $Ca^2s^{2d}$ by the same volume comparison and coarea on the fixed ellipsoid. Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-4-2} bounds $\Delta_z\mathcal F$ above by the wall integral of $(u/r)G(r)^*A_{\mathrm w}G(r)\delta(r)$. The wall current bound and the upper bound for $u/r$ then yield
\[
\Delta_z\mathcal F(T,\tau)\le C(a/s)^2\sigma^me^{-c_0\sigma}\|g_T\|_{p_c}^{p_c}.
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textit{Interior recovery and lower bound.}
Take a center $(X,P,Z)$ with $|W|\le\gamma$, $|Q|\le1/400$. The radius-$h$ ball in the $3n$ real spatial slots about the center fits inside $|W|\le2\gamma$, $|Q|\le1/100$ for sufficiently large $K\gamma$ and $K$: the chart bounds $\nabla W=O(s^{-1})$, $\nabla\Phi=O(1)$ and gives changes at most $Ch/s$ and $Ch$ along such segments. On the ball $|W|\le2\gamma$, so $|W-v|\le4\gamma$ on this enlarged cap, and $\Psi\le C\gamma^2\sigma$. The derivatives through order $M$ in $\eta=h\xi$ are bounded by
\[
B_{\mathrm{inv}}=C_\gamma(hs)^{d/2}\sigma^me^{C\gamma^2\sigma}.
\]

Apply the kernel estimate and Cauchy--Schwarz to this inverse acting on $\mathsf S_0g_T$. At the real center $X$ and any auxiliary point in the ball it gives
\[

\]

\[

\]

Let $\ell$ be the Euclidean distance to the center in the spatial slots. levels.title: Energy estimates on a fixed fiber

levels.component_tex:
Let $n\ge2$, $d=n-1$, and choose an orthonormal spatial frame $X=(x,b)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R$. Put
\[
t=(T+b)/\sqrt2,\qquad s_0=(b-T)/\sqrt2,\qquad \mathsf X=(t,x,s_0).
\]
For a frequency $\xi=(\xi_x,\xi_b)$ with $\xi_b+|\xi|>0$, set
\[
\kappa=(\xi_b+|\xi|)/\sqrt2,\qquad v=\xi_x/\kappa,\qquad
u_{\kappa,v}=c_{\kappa,v}\exp\!\left(\mathrm i\kappa(s_0+v\cdot x-|v|^2t/2)\right),
\]
where $\mathrm i$ is the ordinary Fourier imaginary unit. This is the plane wave of physical phase $X\cdot\xi-T|\xi|$. Let $E_{ab}$ be the elementary $n\times n$ matrix indexed by $0\le a,b\le d$, let
\[
C^t=2E_{00},\qquad C^{x_j}=E_{0j}+E_{j0},\qquad C^{s_0}=-\sum_{j=1}^d E_{jj},
\qquad \mathcal P=\sum_\mu C^\mu\partial_{\mathsf X^\mu},
\]
and put $C(p)=\sum_\mu p_\mu C^\mu$. With $p=\kappa(-|v|^2/2,v,1)$,
\[
-C(p)=\kappa
\begin{pmatrix}|v|^2&-v^{\mathsf t}\\-v&I_d\end{pmatrix},
\qquad -w^{\mathsf t}C(p)w=\kappa|w'-vw_0|^2\quad(w=(w_0,w')\in\mathbb R^n).
\]
The kernel is spanned by $E(v)=(1,v)^{\mathsf t}$, and the entire vector wave
\[
f_{\rm sys}=\sum_{\kappa,v}\kappa^{d/2}E(v)u_{\kappa,v}
\]
solves $\mathcal P f_{\rm sys}=0$. Here the sum ranges over an arbitrary finite set of distinct frequencies $\xi$ with $\xi_b+|\xi|>0$, relabelled by $(\kappa,v)$, and the coefficients $c_{\kappa,v}\in\mathbb C$ are arbitrary. For real states $w_1,w_2\in\mathbb R^n$, let $z=w_1+\mathbf k w_2=(R,\zeta)\in\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}\times\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}^d$, where $\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}=\mathbb R+\mathbf k\mathbb R$ and $\mathbf k^2=-1$. The displacement
\[
q^\mu=\tfrac12\sum_{\ell=1}^2w_\ell^{\mathsf t}C^\mu w_\ell=\tfrac12z^*C^\mu z
\]
multiplies each mode at $\mathsf X-\mathrm i q$ by $e^{p\cdot q}=\exp(-\kappa|\zeta-vR|^2/2)$. For each fixed $R$, the square of $\kappa^{d/2}e^{p\cdot q}$ has integral $\pi^d$ over $\zeta\in\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}^d$ with ordinary Lebesgue measure on its $2d$ real coordinates.

levels.title: Null coordinates, polarization and Gaussian weight

levels.component_tex:
Let $n\ge1$ and let $C^\mu$, $0\le\mu\le n$, be constant real symmetric $n\times n$ matrices. For an open set $\mathcal U\subset\mathbb C^{n+1}$ let $f_{\rm sys}:\mathcal U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic and solve $\sum_\mu C^\mu\partial_{\mathsf X^\mu}f_{\rm sys}=0$. Identify the Fourier complex plane with $\mathbb C_{\mathbf i}\subset\mathbb H$, and use quaternionic units $\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k$ with $\mathbf{ij}=\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf{ki}=\mathbf j$. For $w_1,w_2\in\mathbb R^n$ put $z=w_1+\mathbf k w_2$ and $q^\mu=z^*C^\mu z/2$. Use real $\mathsf X\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$, and put $G=\overline{f_{\rm sys}(\mathsf X-\mathbf i q)}$ on the open set of $(\mathsf X,z)$ where $\mathsf X-\mathbf i q\in\mathcal U$. Add a passive complex coordinate $\eta\in\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}$ and choose a constant $c\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Define
\[
\Theta(z,\eta)_\mu=\tfrac12z^{\mathsf t}C^\mu z+c^\mu\eta,\quad
M_{\mu a}=(C^\mu z)_a,\qquad J=|\det_{\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}}[M,c]|^2.
\]
On the indicated open set, use any local inverse chart at a point with $J>0$ for $(\mathsf X,z,\eta)\mapsto(\mathsf X,\omega)$, where $\omega=\Theta(z,\eta)$. The identities below hold on the image of that chart. Define a quaternionic column $\widetilde\chi$ by
\[
\widetilde\chi_\mu\circ\Theta=J^{-1/2}\sum_aM_{\mu a}\mathbf i G_a.
\]
For a Hermitian quaternionic matrix $A$, write
\[
A^{\mathbb R}_{\mu\alpha,\nu\beta}=\operatorname{Re}(\bar e_\alpha A_{\mu\nu}e_\beta),
\qquad(e_0,e_1,e_2)=(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j),
\]
using the real coordinates of the triples $\mathsf X^\mu+\omega_\mu\mathbf i$. Each real column of $(\widetilde\chi\widetilde\chi^*)^{\mathbb R}$ has zero divergence, and $(\partial_\omega\eta)\widetilde\chi=0$.

levels.title: Conserved density in holomorphic flux coordinates

levels.component_tex:
Apply Lemma~\ref{ms:wave-symbol} to the modes, the system matrices and the displacement. For the map of Lemma~\ref{ms:holomorphic-flux-map}, add the passive coordinate in the $s_0$ slot. With state variables $z=(R,\zeta)$ the map is
\[
(R,\zeta,\eta)\longmapsto(Y,P,S_1)=(R^2,R\zeta,\eta-\zeta\cdot\zeta/2).
\]
On $Y\ne0$, choose a local square root $R$ of $Y$. Then $\zeta=P/R$, $W=\zeta/R$ and $\eta=\Phi$. The complex derivative is block lower triangular with diagonal blocks $2R$, $RI_d$ and $1$. The real volume Jacobian is $J=4|R|^{2d+2}$. Its state derivative $M$ sends $E(v)=(1,v)^{\mathsf t}$ to
\[
(2R,\zeta+Rv,-\zeta\cdot v)^{\mathsf t}=2RV^v.
\]
For a complex vector $w$ write $\ell(w)=(-w\cdot w/2,w,1)$. The phase covector is $\kappa\ell(v)$ and direct contraction gives $\ell(w)V^v=-(w-W)\cdot(w-v)/2$. In particular $\partial\Phi=\ell(W)$ annihilates $V^v$, as does $\ell(v)$. Differentiating $P/Y$ gives $(\partial W)V^v=(v-W)/(2Y)$.

The attenuation in Lemma~\ref{ms:wave-symbol} gives $|\zeta-vR|^2=y|W-v|^2$. Since $2|R|/\sqrt J=y^{-d/2}$, the contribution of the mode to the column $\widetilde\chi$ of Lemma~\ref{ms:holomorphic-flux-map} is
\[
V^v g\mathbf i\,\overline{u_{\kappa,v}}\,m_{\kappa,v},
\qquad g=R/|R|.
\]
Here the Fourier plane has been identified with $\mathbb C_{\mathbf i}$. Multiplying all entries on the right by $(g\mathbf i)^{-1}$ leaves their quaternionic outer product unchanged. Conjugation by $\mathbf i$ fixes the Fourier plane and conjugation by $g$ sends $\mathbf i$ to $g^2\mathbf i=e\mathbf i$, using $\mathbf i c=\bar c\mathbf i$ for $c\in\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}$. The resulting column is exactly $\chi$ in the statement. The formula uses $Y$ itself, so the branch choice disappears. The conservation law is the one in Lemma~\ref{ms:holomorphic-flux-map}. Positivity is immediate from the outer product, and left multiplication by the row $\partial\Phi$ gives zero by the mode identity. The orthogonal change of real index acts in the same way on the three slots, and preserves divergence. The displayed time row follows from $T=(t-s_0)/\sqrt2$.

For fixed $\kappa$ and real $W$, the exponential is a Gaussian centered at $\kappa W$ in transverse frequency $\kappa v$. Since $V_t^v=1$, the null component $A^0_{tt}$ is the squared modulus of the Gaussian-windowed scalar wave at that $\kappa$. For the full wave the sum over $\kappa$ occurs before taking the square.

At a fixed auxiliary point, splitting $V_T^v$ into its real and $\mathbf k$ parts gives $\chi_T=\iota_e(\overline{\mathsf S_0u_{\rm w}})+\mathbf k\iota_e(\overline{\mathsf S_1u_{\rm w}})$. Conjugation by $g$ sends the two orthogonal planes $\mathbb C_{\mathbf i}$ and $\mathbf k\mathbb C_{\mathbf i}$ to the planes of these two terms, since $g$ commutes with $\mathbf k$. This proves the time-component identity. At $W=0$ it gives
\[
2A^0_{TT}=\left|\sum_{\kappa,v}(\kappa/y)^{d/2}
 e^{-\kappa y|v|^2/2}u_{\kappa,v}\right|^2.
\]
levels.section_title: The Euclidean wave current: Proof of Proposition prop-2-2
levels.statement:
Let $n\ge2$, $d=n-1$, $X=(x,b)$ be an orthonormal spatial frame, and $u_{\rm w}=\sum_{\kappa,v}u_{\kappa,v}$ be a finite superposition of forward-wave modes. The sum ranges over an arbitrary finite set of distinct frequencies $\xi=(\xi_x,\xi_b)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R$ with $\xi_b+|\xi|>0$, relabelled by $(\kappa,v)$; each coefficient $c_{\kappa,v}\in\mathbb C$ is arbitrary. For each such frequency set
\[
\kappa=(\xi_b+|\xi|)/\sqrt2>0,\qquad v=\xi_x/\kappa,\qquad
u_{\kappa,v}=c_{\kappa,v}e^{\mathrm i(X\cdot\xi-T|\xi|)}.
\]
Use quaternionic units $\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k$ with $\mathbf{ij}=\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf{ki}=\mathbf j$, and let $\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}=\mathbb R+\mathbf k\mathbb R$. Use null coordinates $\mathsf X=(t,x,s_0)$, with $t=(T+b)/\sqrt2$ and $s_0=(b-T)/\sqrt2$. Denote the corresponding complex auxiliary coordinates by $\omega=(Y,P,S_1)\in\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}\times\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}^d\times\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}$. For $Y\ne0$ set
\[
y=|Y|,\quad e=Y/y,\quad W=P/Y,\quad
\Phi=S_1+\frac{P\cdot P}{2Y},\quad
V^v=\bigl(1,(v+W)/2,-W\cdot v/2\bigr)^{\mathsf t}.
\]
Dots of complex vectors are bilinear. In the physical frame, the auxiliary coordinates are $(\tau,P,Z)$, with $Y=(\tau+Z)/\sqrt2$, $S_1=(Z-\tau)/\sqrt2$. For real $\alpha,\beta$ define $\iota_e(\alpha+\mathrm i\beta)=\alpha+e\mathbf i\beta$. Put
\[
m_{\kappa,v}=(\kappa/y)^{d/2}e^{-\kappa y|W-v|^2/2},\qquad
\chi=\sum_{\kappa,v} V^v\iota_e(\overline{u_{\kappa,v}})m_{\kappa,v},\qquad A^0=\chi\chi^* .
\]
Write $x_{\mu0}=\mathsf X_\mu$ and $\omega_\mu=x_{\mu1}+\mathbf kx_{\mu2}$ in the matching order $\mu=0,\ldots,n$. For a holomorphic scalar or vector function $F$ of $\omega$, write $\partial F$ for its complex Jacobian with columns $\partial_{\omega_\mu}F$, where $\partial_{\omega_\mu}=(\partial_{x_{\mu1}}-\mathbf k\partial_{x_{\mu2}})/2$. Both $\chi$ and $A^0$ are smooth, $A^0\ge0$, and
\[
(\partial\Phi)V^v=0,\qquad
(\partial W)V^v=\frac{v-W}{2Y},\qquad
(\partial\Phi)A^0=0 .
\]
Each real column of $(A^0)^\mathbb R$, with entries
\[
(A^0)^\mathbb R_{\mu\alpha,\nu\beta}=\operatorname{Re}(\bar e_\alpha A^0_{\mu\nu}e_\beta),
\qquad (e_0,e_1,e_2)=(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j),
\]
has zero divergence, meaning that for every column index $(\nu,\beta)$,
\[
 \sum_{\mu=0}^n\sum_{\alpha=0}^2
 \partial_{x_{\mu\alpha}}(A^0)^\mathbb R_{\mu\alpha,\nu\beta}=0.
\]
These conclusions hold in the physical coordinates by the orthogonal change on all three slots. In that frame
\[
V_T^v=(1+W\cdot v/2)/\sqrt2,\qquad A^0_{TT}=|\chi_T|^2.
\]
At a fixed auxiliary point let $\mathsf S_0,\mathsf S_1$ multiply each spatial mode of $u_{\rm w}$ by $b_0m_{\kappa,v},b_1m_{\kappa,v}$, where $b_0,b_1\in\mathbb R$ are defined by $V_T^v=b_0+\mathbf k b_1$. Then
\[
b_0=\frac{1+\operatorname{Re}(W)\cdot v/2}{\sqrt2},
\qquad
b_1=\frac{\operatorname{Im}_{\mathbf k}(W)\cdot v}{2\sqrt2},
\qquad A^0_{TT}=|\mathsf S_0u_{\rm w}|^2+|\mathsf S_1u_{\rm w}|^2.
\]

levels.component_tex:
The wave operator in $(t,x,s_0)$ is $2\partial_t\partial_{s_0}+\Delta_x$, so at frequency $\kappa$ in $s_0$ it becomes $2\mathrm i\kappa\partial_t+\Delta_x$. Substituting $T=(t-s_0)/\sqrt2$ and $b=(t+s_0)/\sqrt2$ into the phase gives the asserted mode because $|\xi|^2-\xi_b^2=|\xi_x|^2$. The first entry of $\mathcal P(\partial_{s_0}\psi,\nabla_x\psi)^{\mathsf t}$ is $(2\partial_t\partial_{s_0}+\Delta_x)\psi$ and the other entries cancel by commutation of derivatives. Evaluating $C(p)$ gives the displayed block matrix. Its quadratic form is the stated square, and its kernel consists of multiples of $E(v)$. On the mode, $\mathcal P$ acts by $\mathrm i C(p)$, yielding the vector solution.

Translation in physical coordinates by $-\mathrm i\rho(1,\omega)$, with $\rho>0$ and $|\omega|=1$, multiplies a mode by $e^{\rho(\xi\cdot\omega-|\xi|)}=e^{-\rho|\xi||\xi/|\xi|-\omega|^2/2}$. At $|\xi|\asymp N$ and $\rho N\gg1$ its angular width is of order $(\rho N)^{-1/2}$. The quadratic flux $q(w)^\mu=w^{\mathsf t}C^\mu w/2$ is $(w_0^2,w_0w',-|w'|^2/2)$ in the null frame. In physical coordinates its time entry and spatial length both equal $(w_0^2+|w'|^2/2)/\sqrt2$. At $w=E(v)$ the physical flux is $(|\xi|,\xi)/\kappa$.

In the sum of the two fluxes, symmetry cancels the mixed terms of $z^*C^\mu z$. Applying the quadratic form for $-C(p)$ to each real state gives $p\cdot q=-\kappa|\zeta-vR|^2/2$. Translating and scaling the integral of $\kappa^d e^{-\kappa|\zeta-vR|^2}$ in $2d$ real coordinates gives $\pi^d$.

Use the tensor $B$ of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-2-1}, extending it by zero in the two passive directions. For a source coordinate $I$ set $Q_I=\mathcal Z_1^I+\mathbf k\mathcal Z_2^I$. The planes $\mathbb C_{\mathbf i}$ and $\mathbf k\mathbb C_{\mathbf i}$ are orthogonal for $\langle u,v\rangle=\operatorname{Re}(u\bar v)$, so $B^{IL}=\operatorname{Re}(Q_I\overline{Q_L})$. Its real and state rows are
\[
Q_{\mathsf X^\mu}=\sum_aM_{\mu a}\mathbf i G_a,\qquad
(Q_{w_{1a}},Q_{w_{2a}})=(G_a,\mathbf k G_a).
\]
Multiplication by $h=h_1+\mathbf k h_2$ on a source auxiliary pair has real rows $(h_1,-h_2)$ and $(h_2,h_1)$, which send $(G_a,\mathbf kG_a)$ to $(\bar hG_a,\mathbf k\bar hG_a)$. The derivative $\partial_{z_a}\Theta_\mu=M_{\mu a}$ follows from the symmetry of $C^\mu$. Together with $-\mathbf i h\mathbf i=\bar h$ for $h\in\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}$, this shows that the target triple of Gram rows is $Q_{\mathsf X^\mu},-\mathbf iQ_{\mathsf X^\mu},-\mathbf jQ_{\mathsf X^\mu}$, with zero contribution from the passive directions. These are the three rows $\bar e_\alpha Q_{\mathsf X^\mu}$ representing a quaternionic outer product.

The real volume Jacobian equals $J$ by holomorphicity. The pushforward as a density under the extended map (which fixes $\mathsf X$) is
\[
\widetilde B\circ\Theta=J^{-1}D\Theta\,B\,D\Theta^{\mathsf t}.
\]
The Gram rows just computed identify $\widetilde B=(\widetilde\chi\widetilde\chi^*)^{\mathbb R}$. Varying $z$ at fixed $\eta$ gives the columns of $M$, so $(\partial_\omega\eta)M=0$ and $(\partial_\omega\eta)\widetilde\chi=0$.

For each target column $K$, test the divergence against a real smooth $\varphi$ of compact support. Changing variables sends the integral to $-\sum_{I,L}\int B^{IL}(\partial_L\Theta^K)\partial_I(\varphi\circ\Theta)$. Integration by parts yields
\[
J(\operatorname{div}\widetilde B)^K\circ\Theta
=\sum_L(\partial_L\Theta^K)(\operatorname{div}B)^L
 +\sum_{I,L} B^{IL}\partial_I\partial_L\Theta^K.
\]
The first sum vanishes by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-2-1}. In the second, both diagonal state blocks are $(\operatorname{Re}(G_a\overline{G_b}))_{ab}$, and the mixed state block vanishes. The real components of $\Theta$ satisfy $\partial_{w_{1a}}\partial_{w_{1b}}\Theta^K+\partial_{w_{2a}}\partial_{w_{2b}}\Theta^K=0$ by the Cauchy--Riemann equations. All terms involving the other coordinates vanish since they enter affinely.

levels.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ and let $C^\mu$, $0\le\mu\le n$, be constant real symmetric $n\times n$ matrices. Identify the Fourier complex plane with $\mathbb C_{\mathbf i}\subset\mathbb H$, and use quaternionic units $\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k$ with $\mathbf{ij}=\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf{ki}=\mathbf j$. For $w_1,w_2\in\mathbb R^n$ put $z=w_1+\mathbf k w_2$ and $q^\mu=z^*C^\mu z/2$. Use real $\mathsf X\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$, and put $G=\overline{f_{\rm sys}(\mathsf X-\mathbf i q)}$ on the open set of $(\mathsf X,z)$ where $\mathsf X-\mathbf i q\in\mathcal U$. \[
\Theta(z,\eta)_\mu=\tfrac12z^{\mathsf t}C^\mu z+c^\mu\eta,\quad
M_{\mu a}=(C^\mu z)_a,\qquad J=|\det_{\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}}[M,c]|^2.

\[

\[

\]
using the real coordinates of the triples $\mathsf X^\mu+\omega_\mu\mathbf i$. Each real column of $(\widetilde\chi\widetilde\chi^*)^{\mathbb R}$ has zero divergence, and $(\partial_\omega\eta)\widetilde\chi=0$.

levels.component_tex:
For real states $a,b$ the flux $a^{\mathsf t}C^\mu b$ has divergence $(\mathcal P a)^{\mathsf t}b+a^{\mathsf t}\mathcal P b$ by the product rule and symmetry, the bilinear conservation identity of \cite{r-25}. Its value at $(w_\ell,\delta w_\ell)$ is the derivative of $q^\mu$ in the $\delta w_\ell$ direction. In the tube coordinates $\mathsf X-\mathrm i q$ (compare \cite{r-6}, Section~1), direct differentiation shows that $D_{\ell a}$ annihilates each component of $\mathsf X-\mathrm i q$. Hence $D_{\ell a}\overline G=0$, and conjugation gives $\partial_{w_{\ell a}}G=\mathrm i V_{\ell a}G$. Each $D_{\ell a}$ has zero divergence since its state coefficients are constant and its spatial coefficients have no $\mathsf X$ dependence. Thus
\[
\operatorname{div}\mathcal Z_\ell=2\mathrm i\sum_aV_{\ell a}G_a
=2\mathrm i w_\ell^{\mathsf t}\mathcal P G=0.
\]
Here $\mathcal P G=0$ follows by differentiation in $\mathsf X$ and conjugation, since the matrices are real.

For the ordinary flat connection, $D_{\ell a}\overline G=0$ leaves only $D_{\ell a}$ acting on the coefficients of $\overline{D_{mb}}$ in the following computation:
\[
\nabla_{\mathcal Z_\ell}\overline{\mathcal Z_m}
=-\mathrm i\delta_{\ell m}\sum_\mu(G^{\mathsf t}C^\mu\overline G)\partial_{\mathsf X^\mu}.
\]
Indeed the derivative of the coefficient $(C^\mu w_m)_b$ in direction $w_{\ell a}$ is $\delta_{\ell m}(C^\mu)_{ba}$. The vector multiplying $-\mathrm i\delta_{\ell m}$ is real by the symmetry of $C^\mu$. The product rule gives $\operatorname{div}(\mathcal Z_\ell\otimes\overline{\mathcal Z_\ell})=(\operatorname{div}\mathcal Z_\ell)\overline{\mathcal Z_\ell}+\nabla_{\mathcal Z_\ell}\overline{\mathcal Z_\ell}$, whose real part vanishes. Writing $\mathcal Z_\ell=A_\ell+\mathrm iB_\ell$ with real fields exhibits the summand as $A_\ell\otimes A_\ell+B_\ell\otimes B_\ell$ after taking real parts. The imaginary part of the same flat-connection identity gives $[A_\ell,B_\ell]=\sum_\mu(G^{\mathsf t}C^\mu\overline G)\partial_{\mathsf X^\mu}$.

Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-2-2} identifies $m_0$ as the multiplier symbol. Since $|\xi|^2-\xi_b^2=|\xi_x|^2$ and $|\xi|+\xi_b=\sqrt2\kappa$,
\[
 |\xi|=\kappa(1+|v|^2/2)/\sqrt2 .
\]
The annulus bounds and $|v|\le1/10$ give $\kappa\asymp h^{-1}$. The bound $|\operatorname{Re}(W)\cdot v|\le1/100$ gives $b_0\asymp1$. Inverting $m_0$ gives the claimed reciprocal. If $y\asymp h$, then $\Psi$ is bounded and $(\kappa/y)^{d/2}\asymp h^{-d}$, giving the two-sided bound.

Pairwise disjoint lattice cubes centered on points of the ball, of side $2\pi/100$, fit inside a ball of radius $C_0/h+\pi\sqrt n/100$. levels.section_title: Wave multiplier on a torus frequency cap: Proof of Lemma wave-cap-estimates
levels.statement:
Let $n\ge2$, $d=n-1$, $0<h\le1$, and $0<c_0<C_0$. In any orthonormal frame $(x,b)$ on the covering space of $\mathbb T^n=\mathbb R^n/(100\mathbb Z^n)$, write $\xi=(\xi_x,\xi_b)$ and $\kappa=(\xi_b+|\xi|)/\sqrt2$. For frequencies with $\kappa>0$ put $v=\xi_x/\kappa$, and assume $c_0\le h|\xi|\le C_0$ and $|v|\le1/10$. For $y>0$ and $W\in\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}^d$ with $|W|\le1/10$, where $\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}=\mathbb R+\mathbf k\mathbb R$ and $\mathbf k^2=-1$, let
\[
 b_0=\frac{1+\operatorname{Re}(W)\cdot v/2}{\sqrt2},\qquad
 \Psi=\kappa y|W-v|^2/2,\qquad
 m_0=b_0(\kappa/y)^{d/2}e^{-\Psi}.
\]
Write $\mathsf S_0$ for the multiplier that multiplies the coefficient at $\xi$ by $m_0$. On these frequencies, $\kappa\asymp h^{-1}$, $b_0\asymp1$, and
\[
 m_0^{-1}=b_0^{-1}(y/\kappa)^{d/2}e^\Psi
     \asymp(hy)^{d/2}e^\Psi .
\]
In particular $h^d m_0\asymp1$ if $y\asymp h$.

If $f(X)=\sum_\xi c_\xi e^{\mathrm i X\cdot\xi}$ is a trigonometric polynomial on $\mathbb T^n$ supported on these frequencies, then the number of supported frequencies is $O(h^{-n})$ and $\sum_\xi|c_\xi|\lesssim h^{-n/2}\|f\|_2$. The norm uses ordinary torus volume. The estimates are uniform in the frame, with constants depending on $n,c_0,C_0$ and, for the two-sided bound when $y\asymp h$, the fixed comparison constants for $y/h$.

levels.component_tex:
The rank-one perturbation of the Moore determinant follows from the diagonal perturbation formula and unitary invariance below. The proof will differentiate the resulting formula to identify the corresponding cofactor.

\begin{Proposition}[Alesker, Theorem 1.1.9(ii) and Proposition 1.1.11]\label{ext:alesker-determinant}
Let $\mathbb H$ be the real associative algebra with unit $1$ and basis $(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k)$, with $\mathbf i^2=\mathbf j^2=\mathbf k^2=\mathbf i\mathbf j\mathbf k=-1$. Conjugation fixes the real coefficient and negates the other three. On quaternionic columns use right scalar multiplication and inner product $v^*w$, with $^*$ denoting conjugate transpose.

For $m\ge1$, every quaternionic $m\times m$ matrix $A=A^*$ has a quaternionic orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m$ by Claim~1.1.7 of \cite{r-2}. For each real $\lambda$, the number of entries equal to $\lambda$ in this list is $\dim_{\mathbb H}\ker(A-\lambda I_m)$, so the list with multiplicities is independent of the basis up to order. Define the Moore determinant by
\[
 \det A=\prod_{a=1}^m\lambda_a.
\]
Thus $\det I_m=1$. The unitary invariance of Theorem~1.1.9(ii) and the real diagonal formula of Example~1.1.10(a) in \cite{r-2} identify this product with the normalized determinant of Theorem~1.1.8. For every quaternionic $m\times m$ matrix $U$ with $U^*U=I_m$ and every real diagonal $T=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\ldots,t_m)$,
\[
 \det(U^*AU)=\det A,\qquad
 \det(A+T)=\sum_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}}
          \left(\prod_{i\in I}t_i\right)\det A_{I^c,I^c}.
\]
Here $A_{I^c,I^c}$ is the principal submatrix on $I^c$ and the determinant of the empty matrix is one. See \cite{r-2}, pp.~7--8, for the normalization and the identities.
\end{Proposition}

The pairing is real, symmetric and nondegenerate on Hermitian matrices, since the real trace is cyclic and $\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A^2)$ is the sum of the squared entry norms. In the real representation on $\mathbb R^{4m}$ every eigenvalue occurs four times. For $A>0$, $\log\det A$ is one quarter of the real log determinant. The rank-one perturbation of the Moore determinant follows from the diagonal perturbation formula and unitary invariance below. The proof will differentiate the resulting formula to identify the corresponding cofactor.

\begin{Proposition}[Alesker, Theorem 1.1.9(ii) and Proposition 1.1.11]\label{ext:alesker-determinant}
Let $\mathbb H$ be the real associative algebra with unit $1$ and basis $(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k)$, with $\mathbf i^2=\mathbf j^2=\mathbf k^2=\mathbf i\mathbf j\mathbf k=-1$. Conjugation fixes the real coefficient and negates the other three. On quaternionic columns use right scalar multiplication and inner product $v^*w$, with $^*$ denoting conjugate transpose.

For $m\ge1$, every quaternionic $m\times m$ matrix $A=A^*$ has a quaternionic orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m$ by Claim~1.1.7 of \cite{r-2}. For each real $\lambda$, the number of entries equal to $\lambda$ in this list is $\dim_{\mathbb H}\ker(A-\lambda I_m)$, so the list with multiplicities is independent of the basis up to order. Define the Moore determinant by
\[
 \det A=\prod_{a=1}^m\lambda_a.
\]
Thus $\det I_m=1$. The unitary invariance of Theorem~1.1.9(ii) and the real diagonal formula of Example~1.1.10(a) in \cite{r-2} identify this product with the normalized determinant of Theorem~1.1.8. \[

 \det(A+T)=\sum_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}}
          \left(\prod_{i\in I}t_i\right)\det A_{I^c,I^c}.
\]
Here $A_{I^c,I^c}$ is the principal submatrix on $I^c$ and the determinant of the empty matrix is one. See \cite{r-2}, pp.~7--8, for the normalization and the identities.
\end{Proposition}

levels.section_title: Moore determinant and cofactor identities: Proof of Lemma lemma-3-2
levels.statement:
For Hermitian quaternionic $m\times m$ matrices set $A:B=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(AB)$. Write $\det A$ for the Moore determinant, the product of the real eigenvalues counted with quaternionic multiplicity. It is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $m$. Its cofactor $C(A)$ is the Hermitian matrix determined by
\[
C(A):B=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\det(A+tB)\right|_{t=0}.
\]
It is polynomial of degree $m-1$, with $C(A)=(\det A)A^{-1}$ for $A>0$. For $A\ge0$ one has $C(A)\ge0$, and when $A$ is also singular, $C(A)$ kills the image of $A$. On positive definite matrices $\log\det$ is concave and increasing in the matrix order.

For every Hermitian $A$, unit vector $v\in\mathbb H^m$ and real $t$,
\[
v^*C(A)v=\det(A|_{v^\perp}),\qquad
\det(A+tvv^*)=\det A+t\,v^*C(A)v,
\]
where $A|_{v^\perp}$ is compression to the quaternionic orthogonal complement and the determinant in dimension zero is one. For a Hermitian $M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\ell&c^*\\c&D\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $D>0$, put $\sigma=\ell-c^*D^{-1}c$ and let $v_0$ be the first coordinate vector. Then
\[
\det M=(\det D)\sigma,\qquad M-\sigma v_0v_0^*\ge0.
\]

levels.component_tex:
Commutation of the real derivatives gives Hermitian symmetry. In a diagonal entry the terms for $\alpha\ne\beta$ cancel in pairs, and each term with $\alpha=\beta$ has coefficient one. This gives the trace. Applying the Hessian map to $\xi\xi^{\mathsf t}$ gives $gg^*$. Every nonnegative real form is a sum of such forms. The ordinary product rule gives the identity for $H(uv)$. In four slots, the real transpose of a quaternionic unitary $U$ acts on the encoded covector by $U^*$. The rank-one calculation yields $H(u\circ U)=U^*(H(u)\circ U)U$ and linearity extends the calculation to any real Hessian. Real orthogonal matrices on the coordinate index preserve the three-slot subspace, giving the covariance there.

Write $P_a=p_a+\mathbf k q_a$, so $2\partial_{\bar P_a}=\partial_{p_a}+\mathbf k\partial_{q_a}$. Since $\mathbf{ki}=\mathbf j$, the gradient is $2(\partial_{\bar P_a}u)\mathbf i$. In the Hessian the four coefficients for derivatives $(p_ap_b,p_aq_b,q_ap_b,q_aq_b)$ are $1,-\mathbf k,\mathbf k,1$, giving $4\partial_{\bar P_a}\partial_{P_b}u$. For holomorphic $F$, the complex chain rule gives
\[
\partial_{\bar P_a}\partial_{P_b}\sum_\nu|F_\nu|^2
 =\sum_\nu\overline{J_{\nu a}}\,J_{\nu b},\qquad
G(\rho\circ F)=2J^*(\partial_{\bar F_\nu}\rho)_\nu\,\mathbf i,
\]
where the derivatives of $\rho$ are evaluated at $F(P)$.
levels.section_title: Quaternionic Hessian calculus: Proof of Lemma lemma-3-1
levels.statement:
Let $k=3$ or $4$, use $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k)$, and write $z_a=\sum_{\alpha=0}^{k-1}e_\alpha z_{a\alpha}$ for $1\le a\le m$. For a real $C^2$ function $u$, define
\[
G_a(u)=\sum_\alpha e_\alpha\partial_{a\alpha}u,\qquad
H_{ab}(u)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}e_\alpha\bar e_\beta\,
       \partial_{a\alpha}\partial_{b\beta}u,\qquad
\partial_{a\alpha}=\partial/\partial z_{a\alpha}.
\]
Then $H(u)$ is Hermitian and $\operatorname{tr}H(u)=\Delta u$. The map from the real Hessian to $H(u)$ sends the real rank-one matrix $\xi\xi^{\mathsf t}$ to $gg^*$, where $g_a=\sum_\alpha e_\alpha\xi_{a\alpha}$, and sends nonnegative real matrices to nonnegative quaternionic matrices. For real $C^2$ functions $u,v$,
\[
H(uv)=uH(v)+vH(u)+G(u)G(v)^*+G(v)G(u)^* .
\]
In four slots $H$ is covariant under quaternionic unitary changes of coordinates, and in three slots it is covariant under real orthogonal changes of the index $a$ applied in all slots. If $u$ depends only on $P\in\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}^m$ in $z_a=x_a+P_a\mathbf i$ (and is independent of the fourth slot if present), write $P_a=p_a+\mathbf k q_a$ and use
\[
\partial_{P_a}=\tfrac12(\partial_{p_a}-\mathbf k\partial_{q_a}),\qquad
\partial_{\bar P_a}=\tfrac12(\partial_{p_a}+\mathbf k\partial_{q_a}).
\]
With this convention,
\[
G_a(u)=2(\partial_{\bar P_a}u)\mathbf i,\qquad
H_{ab}(u)=4\partial_{\bar P_a}\partial_{P_b}u .
\]
For a holomorphic map $F=(F_1,\ldots,F_\ell)$ of $P$ with complex Jacobian $J_{\nu a}=\partial_{P_a}F_\nu$, one has $H(\sum_\nu|F_\nu|^2)=4J^*J$. For a smooth real function $\rho$ of the complex variables $F_\nu$, the gradient $G(\rho\circ F)$ belongs to the quaternionic image of $J^*$.

levels.component_tex:
Solving the definitions of $Y,W,\Phi$ gives the stated inverse. Its denominator is bounded away from zero on $|W|\le w_0$, and $|aQ|\le a/10<s/10$ gives $|Y|\asymp s$. The formulas thus give inverse holomorphic maps on neighborhoods of the closed fibers and depend smoothly on $\tau$.

Set $F=(W/w_0,10Q)$ and let $J$ be its complex Jacobian in $(\tau,P,Z)$, with spatial submatrix $J_{\rm fib}$. Since $r=|F|^2-1$, Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-1} gives $H(r)=4J^*J$ and $G(r)=2J^*F\mathbf i$. The matrix $J_{\rm fib}$ is invertible. In the full space the complex direction acquired by varying $\tau$ at fixed $(W,Q)$ spans $\ker J$ over $\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}$. Its quaternionic span is the full kernel of $H(r)$, as the rank of $J$ over $\mathbb H$ is $n$ by the invertible spatial submatrix. This kernel is orthogonal to $G(r)\in\operatorname{im}J^*$ and is contained in the kernel of $H(|\Phi|^2)$, since the last row of $J$ is a nonzero multiple of $\partial\Phi$. In the inverse chart the derivatives of $(P,Z)$ in $W$ are $O(s)$ and those in $Q$ are $O(a)$. This gives $\|J_{\rm fib}^{-1}\|\lesssim s$ and the lower Hessian bound. For the gradient bound, use $|F|\le1$ to get
\[
  G_{\rm fib}(r)G_{\rm fib}(r)^*=4J_{\rm fib}^*FF^*J_{\rm fib}
     \le4J_{\rm fib}^*J_{\rm fib}.
\]

At fixed $\tau$ the complex Jacobian determinant of the inverse chart is $\sqrt 2\,aY^d/(1+W\cdot W/2)$. Indeed the exterior product of the $d$ differentials of $P=WY$ with $\mathrm dY$ leaves only $Y^d$ times the $d$ differentials of $W$ wedged with $\mathrm dY$, while $\mathrm dZ=\sqrt 2\,\mathrm dY$ and $\partial_Q Y=a/(1+W\cdot W/2)$. Squaring its absolute value gives the volume estimate. The quaternionic determinant of $H_{\rm fib}(r)$ is $4^n|\det_{\mathbb C}J_{\rm fib}|^2$, since the positive complex Hermitian matrix $J_{\rm fib}^*J_{\rm fib}$ has the same eigenvalues as a quaternionic Hermitian matrix. This proves the determinant estimate. The spatial derivatives of $\Phi$ are bounded and $\partial_Z\Phi=(1-W\cdot W/2)/\sqrt2$ is bounded away from zero, which proves the rank and eigenvalue assertion by the holomorphic Hessian formula. All first derivatives of $W=P/Y$ are $O(s^{-1})$, so the bound on $|G(|W|^2)|$ follows.
levels.section_title: Fiber geometry: Proof of Lemma lemma-4-1
levels.statement:
Let $n\ge2$, $d=n-1$, $w_0=1/10$, $a>0$, $s=|\tau|$, and $z=(T,\tau)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}$ with $a<s<4$. At fixed $z$, write $X\in\mathbb R^n/(100\mathbb Z^n)$ and $(P,Z)\in\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}^d\times\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}$. On $Y\ne0$ define
\[
 Y=(\tau+Z)/\sqrt 2,\qquad W=P/Y,\qquad
 \Phi=(Z-\tau)/\sqrt 2+(P\cdot P)/(2Y),\qquad Q=\Phi/a .
\]
Here the dot denotes the complex bilinear product and the norm is Euclidean. Let $\Omega_z$ be the fiber $r<0$ in this open set, where $r=|W|^2/w_0^2+100|Q|^2-1$, and put
$\Omega=\{(z,X,P,Z):a<s<4,\ (X,P,Z)\in\Omega_z\}$. For the full operators use $n+1$ real triples $x_{j0}+x_{j1}\mathbf i+x_{j2}\mathbf j$ with real slots $(T,X)$ and auxiliary slots given by $(\tau,P,Z)\mathbf i$, in matching index order. Thus if an auxiliary coordinate is $p+\mathbf kq$, its slots are $(x_{j1},x_{j2})=(p,q)$. Write $(e_0,e_1,e_2)=(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j)$, $\partial_{j\alpha}=\partial/\partial x_{j\alpha}$, and set
\[
G_j(v)=\sum_{\alpha=0}^2 e_\alpha\partial_{j\alpha}v,\qquad
H_{jk}(v)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta=0}^2 e_\alpha\bar e_\beta\partial_{j\alpha}\partial_{k\beta}v.
\]
The spatial operators $G_{\rm fib},H_{\rm fib}$ use only the $n$ indices belonging to $(X,P,Z)$ at fixed $(T,\tau)$. Write $\mathrm d\zeta=\mathrm dX\,\mathrm dP\,\mathrm dZ$ for ordinary fiber volume.

The fiber chart $(P,Z)\mapsto(W,Q)$ is a biholomorphism to the ellipsoid $|W|^2/w_0^2+100|Q|^2<1$ and extends to neighborhoods of the closures. Its inverse is
\[
 Y=\frac{\sqrt 2\,\tau+aQ}{1+W\cdot W/2},\qquad P=WY,\qquad Z=\sqrt 2\,Y-\tau .
\]
On the closed fibers, uniformly for $a<s<4$, one has $|Y|\asymp s$ and
\begin{align*}
 H_{\rm fib}(r)&\ge c s^{-2}I,
 &G_{\rm fib}(r)G_{\rm fib}(r)^*&\le H_{\rm fib}(r),\\
 \mathrm dP\,\mathrm dZ&\asymp a^2s^{2d}\,\mathrm dW\,\mathrm dQ,
 &\det H_{\rm fib}(r)&\asymp a^{-2}s^{-2d}.
\end{align*}
The full $H(r)$ is positive semidefinite with a one-dimensional quaternionic kernel contained in $G(r)^\perp\cap\ker H(|\Phi|^2)$. The spatial $H_{\rm fib}(|\Phi|^2)$ has rank one and nonzero eigenvalue comparable to one. The full gradient satisfies $|G(|W|^2)|\lesssim s^{-1}$.

levels.title: Fiber geometry

levels.component_tex:
Let $m\ge1$ and let $\widetilde\Omega$ be the flat product of a torus of dimension $2m$ and a bounded smooth domain in $\mathbb R^{2m}$, with compact closure, with real coordinates grouped in quaternionic quadruples. Index the slots by $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k)$. The torus directions occupy slots $0$ and $3$, along $e_0=1$ and $e_3=\mathbf k$, and the bounded domain occupies slots $1$ and $2$. For real slot derivatives $\partial_{a\alpha}$, set
\[
G_a(v)=\sum_{\alpha=0}^3e_\alpha\partial_{a\alpha}v,\qquad
H_{ab}(v)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta=0}^3e_\alpha\bar e_\beta\,\partial_{a\alpha}\partial_{b\beta}v.
\]
Let $r$ be a smooth defining function, negative inside, with nonzero boundary gradient and $H(r)>0$ on the closure. Let $B_0$ be smooth with $H(B_0)\ge0$, and let $g$ be smooth with $g>\det H(B_0)$ there. Use the Moore determinant and set
\[
g_t=(1-t)\det H(B_0+r)+t g,\qquad 0\le t\le1 .
\]
There are $b\ge b'>0$ and a constant $C$, depending only on the fixed domain and the data $r,B_0,g$, such that any smooth solution $\psi=B_0+u$ of
\[
H(\psi)>0,\qquad \det H(\psi)=g_t,\qquad u|_{\partial\widetilde\Omega}=0
\]
with positivity up to the boundary satisfies
\[
br\le u\le b'r,\qquad \|\psi\|_{C^2(\overline{\widetilde\Omega})}\le C .
\]
All three constants are independent of $t$.

Work first on the compact quotient with boundary $\widetilde\Omega=\Omega\times(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^m$, extending the data constantly in the new periodic directions. In the four-slot basis $(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k)$ with indices $0,1,2,3$, the original periods $\Lambda$ are in slot $0$ and the new periods $\mathbb Z^m$ are in slot $3$. Regrouping the real coordinates identifies $\widetilde\Omega$ with the torus $\mathbb R^{2m}/(\Lambda\times\mathbb Z^m)$ in slots $0,3$ times $V$ in slots $1,2$. Until descent, $G,H$ are the full four-slot gradient and Hessian. Write $\mathcal H(D^2\psi)=H(\psi)$, and write $\widehat\xi$ for a real covector $\xi$ encoded as a quaternionic column by its four slots. Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-1} gives $\mathcal H(\xi\xi^{\mathsf t})=\widehat\xi\widehat\xi^*$, $\operatorname{tr}H(\psi)=\Delta\psi$, and covariance under quaternionic unitary coordinate transformations.

\emph{Comparison and continuation.} Join the known solution $u=r$ to the desired density by
\[
 g_t=(1-t)\det H(B_0+r)+tg,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\]
At a solution $\psi=B_0+u$, put $Q=H(\psi)$ and $S=\operatorname{tr}Q^{-1}$. By Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2}, the derivative of the log determinant and its real principal symbol are
\[
 Lw=Q^{-1}:H(w),\qquad \sigma_L(\xi)=\widehat\xi^*Q^{-1}\widehat\xi .
\]
Thus $L$ is uniformly elliptic at any fixed smooth solution with $Q>0$ on the compact closure. If $Q_i=H(\psi_i)>0$ for two potentials, interpolate the matrices to obtain
\[
 \log\det Q_1-\log\det Q_2=
 \left(\int_0^1((1-\theta)Q_2+\theta Q_1)^{-1}\,\mathrm d\theta\right):H(\psi_1-\psi_2).
\]
The averaged real operator is uniformly elliptic when the Hessians are positive up to the boundary. The maximum principle proves the comparison assertion in four slots and implies uniqueness. The same argument holds for a bounded subdomain or a compact quotient with boundary.

For each $k\ge0$ and $0<\alpha<1$, the linearized Dirichlet operator $L:C_0^{k+2,\alpha}\to C^{k,\alpha}$ is an isomorphism, where the subscript means zero boundary trace. The local linear Schauder estimates and Dirichlet theory of \cite{r-31}, Theorems 6.14 and 6.19, apply in a finite cover of the flat quotient. In the method of continuity from the Laplacian to $L$, the defining function $r$ is a common strict barrier since $H(r)\ge cI$. The maximum principle gives the uniform $C^0$ estimate for this linear interpolation, the Schauder estimates give the corresponding higher bounds, and the initial Dirichlet Laplacian is invertible. The implicit function theorem applied to the nonlinear equation now proves openness of the set of solvable $t$.

With this product and the four-slot Hessian, Lemma~\ref{ms:dirichlet-c2} provides the two barriers and the uniform full $C^2$ estimate for each smooth solution on this path.

\emph{Regularity, descent and dependence on parameters.} The $C^2$ bound and $\det Q=g_t\ge c_0>0$ give $cI\le Q\le CI$. Thus the real Hessians lie in the compact convex set
\[
 \mathcal K=\{M:|M|\le C_1,\ cI\le\mathcal H(M)\le CI\}.
\]
On $\mathcal H(M)>0$ the smooth function $F(M)=\log\det\mathcal H(M)$ is concave by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2}. For $M\in\mathcal K$ one has
\[
 DF(M)[\xi\xi^{\mathsf t}]=
 \widehat\xi^*\mathcal H(M)^{-1}\widehat\xi
 \in[C^{-1}|\xi|^2,c^{-1}|\xi|^2].
\]
These are the uniform real ellipticity and concavity hypotheses on $\mathcal K$ in the interior and boundary estimates of \cite{r-31}, Theorems 17.14 and $17.26'$, hypotheses (i)$'$ and (ii)$'$. Schauder bootstrapping yields smoothness up to the boundary: after flattening, differentiate tangentially with the specified Dirichlet data and recover the pure normal second derivative from the equation by uniform ellipticity. The implicit function theorem in each $C_0^{k+2,\alpha}$ proves smooth dependence up to the boundary. The strict determinant inequalities choosing $b,b'$ persist locally for the family.

levels.component_tex:
Put $Q=H(\psi)$, $S=\operatorname{tr}Q^{-1}$ and
$Lw=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(Q^{-1}H(w))$. The rank-one Hessian rule of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-1} shows that the real principal symbol is $\widehat\xi^*Q^{-1}\widehat\xi$ for the four-slot encoding $\widehat\xi$ of a real covector. The comparison principle follows by integrating the derivative of $\log\det$ along the straight segment of two positive Hessians. The averaged operator has positive definite real symbol on the compact closure, so the maximum principle applies. The formulas for differentiating $\log\det$ and its concavity are those of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2}.

Both endpoint densities are strictly above $\det H(B_0)$, with a uniform positive gap by compactness. Choose $0<b'<1<b$ so that
\[
 \det H(B_0+b'r)<g_t<\det H(B_0+br)
 \quad\text{on }\overline{\widetilde\Omega},\quad 0\le t\le1.
\]
The lower inequality follows from the gap by taking $b'$ small, and the upper one from $H(r)\ge cI$ by taking $b$ large. The comparison principle gives $br\le u\le b'r$. Smooth division in a boundary collar gives $u=\alpha_0r$ with $b'\le\alpha_0\le b$, so $\nabla u=\alpha_0\nabla r$ on the boundary. Also $Lr\ge cS$, and the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality gives $S\ge mg_t^{-1/m}\ge c_0>0$. For any constant real unit direction $e$, differentiating once and using concavity on differentiating twice gives
\[
 L\psi_e=(\log g_t)_e,\qquad L\psi_{ee}\ge(\log g_t)_{ee}.
\]
The maximum principle for $\pm\psi_e+Cr$ bounds all gradients from their boundary values, already bounded by the barriers and the data. Applied to $\psi_{ee}+Cr$, it reduces the upper real Hessian bound to a boundary estimate.

\emph{Boundary second derivatives.} In a flat chart centered at a boundary point let $\nu$ be the outward real unit normal, identified with its quaternionic column. Tangential real directions $v,w$ satisfy $D^2u(v,w)=\alpha_0D^2r(v,w)$ at the center. For a mixed derivative fix a real unit tangent $e$ and construct a local quaternionic rigid-motion field $X=(e+Ax)\cdot\nabla$ by setting
\[
 v=\frac{P_{\rm tan}D^2r\,e}{|\nabla r|},\qquad
 A=v\nu^*-\nu v^*-\nu(\nu^*v)\nu^* .
\]
Here $P_{\rm tan}$ is the real tangent projection. As $\operatorname{Re}(\nu^*v)=0$, one has $A^*=-A$ and $A\nu=v$. At the center $Xr=0$ and for every real tangent $w$,
\[
 \partial_w(Xr)=D^2r(w,e)-|\nabla r|\,w\cdot A\nu=0.
\]
In particular $|Xu|=|\alpha_0Xr|\le C|x|^2$ along the boundary in the chart. The rigid-motion flow acts by quaternionic unitary rotations and translations. Covariance gives $L(X\psi)=X\log g_t$: any commutator from conjugating $Q$ pairs to zero with $Q^{-1}$. Subtract $L(XB_0)$ to get $|L(Xu)|\le CS$, using the smooth data and $S\ge c_0$.

In a small fixed chart ball take $w_0=C_1|x|^2-C_2r$. First choose $C_1$ large so $w_0\ge|Xu|$ on the true boundary by the quadratic bound and on the spherical boundary by the gradient bound. Then take $C_2$ large enough for $L(w_0\pm Xu)\le0$, using $H(|x|^2)=8I$ and $Lr\ge cS$. The minimum principle gives $|Xu|\le w_0$. Both vanish at the center, so the bound controls $|\partial_\nu Xu|$ there. This is $|D^2u(\nu,e)|$, because the extra term $\nabla u\cdot A\nu$ vanishes with $\nabla u$ normal and $A\nu$ tangent. Compactness makes the estimates uniform over the boundary.

By the product rule of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-1}, at the boundary
\[
 H(u)=\alpha_0H(r)+G(\alpha_0)G(r)^*+G(r)G(\alpha_0)^*,
 \qquad G(r)=|\nabla r|\nu .
\]
The cross terms vanish on the quaternionic orthogonal complement of $\nu$. Thus $Q$ compressed to $\nu^\perp$ is bounded below by $b'H(r)|_{\nu^\perp}\ge cI$. In a quaternionic orthonormal basis beginning with $\nu$, the real rank-one Hessian rule therefore gives
\[
 Q=\begin{pmatrix}\psi_{\nu\nu}+c_1&z^*\\z&D\end{pmatrix},
\]
where $c_1,z,D$ depend only on the already bounded real tangential or mixed second derivatives. For $m>1$, Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2} gives
\[
 \psi_{\nu\nu}=g_t/\det D+z^*D^{-1}z-c_1,
\]
which is bounded because $D\ge cI$. For $m=1$ use $Q=g_t$. The upper Hessian estimate in the interior now gives $D^2\psi\le CI$. Since $\Delta\psi=\operatorname{tr}Q>0$, every real Hessian eigenvalue is bounded below by $-(4m-1)C$. This proves a uniform full $C^2$ bound.

levels.statement:
Let $m\ge1$ and let $\widetilde\Omega$ be the flat product of a torus of dimension $2m$ and a bounded smooth domain in $\mathbb R^{2m}$, with compact closure, with real coordinates grouped in quaternionic quadruples. Index the slots by $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k)$. The torus directions occupy slots $0$ and $3$, along $e_0=1$ and $e_3=\mathbf k$, and the bounded domain occupies slots $1$ and $2$. For real slot derivatives $\partial_{a\alpha}$, set
\[
G_a(v)=\sum_{\alpha=0}^3e_\alpha\partial_{a\alpha}v,\qquad
H_{ab}(v)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta=0}^3e_\alpha\bar e_\beta\,\partial_{a\alpha}\partial_{b\beta}v.
\]

\[
g_t=(1-t)\det H(B_0+r)+t g,\qquad 0\le t\le1 .
\]

\[
H(\psi)>0,\qquad \det H(\psi)=g_t,\qquad u|_{\partial\widetilde\Omega}=0
\]
with positivity up to the boundary satisfies
\[
br\le u\le b'r,\qquad \|\psi\|_{C^2(\overline{\widetilde\Omega})}\le C .
\]
All three constants are independent of $t$.

Let $k=3$ or $4$, $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k)$, and let $u$ be a smooth real function of real coordinates $z_{a\alpha}$ with $1\le a\le m$ and $0\le\alpha<k$. Define $H_{ab}(u)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}e_\alpha\bar e_\beta\,\partial_{a\alpha}\partial_{b\beta}u$, with $\partial_{a\alpha}=\partial/\partial z_{a\alpha}$. For a quaternionic Hermitian $A$, let $C(A)$ be the derivative of its Moore determinant under the real pairing $\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(AB)$. Then
\[
\sum_{a,\alpha}\bar e_\alpha\,\partial_{a\alpha} C(H(u))_{ab}=0
\qquad(1\le b\le m).
\]

levels.component_tex:
Let $n\ge2$, $d=n-1$, $h>0$, $K\ge1$, $a=Kh$, and $w_0=1/10$. Use $T\in\mathbb R$ and $X\in\mathbb T^n=\mathbb R^n/(100\mathbb Z^n)$, with spatial frame $X=(x,b)$ on the covering space, $x\in\mathbb R^d$, $b\in\mathbb R$. The auxiliary coordinates are $(\tau,P,Z)\in\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}\times\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}^d\times\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}$, where $\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}=\mathbb R+\mathbf k\mathbb R$. For $Y=(\tau+Z)/\sqrt2\ne0$ define
\[
 W=P/Y,\qquad \Phi=(Z-\tau)/\sqrt2+(P\cdot P)/(2Y),\qquad
 Q=\Phi/a,\qquad r=|W|^2/w_0^2+100|Q|^2-1 .
\]
The dot is the complex bilinear product and the norms are Euclidean. For $z=(T,\tau)$ with $a<s=|\tau|<4$, let
\[
 \Omega_z=\{(X,P,Z)\in\mathbb T^n\times\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}^d\times\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}:Y\ne0,\ r<0\}.
\]
For the full operators let $j=0$ correspond to $T$ and $\tau$, $1\le j\le d$ to $x_j$ and $P_j$, and $j=n$ to $b$ and $Z$. In each triple $x_{j0}$ is the real spacetime coordinate, and $x_{j1},x_{j2}$ are the coefficients of $1,\mathbf k$ in its corresponding auxiliary coordinate. The spatial slot-$0$ derivatives are taken along the chosen frame on the covering space and act on periodic functions. Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2)=(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j)$, with $\mathbf k\mathbf i=\mathbf j$, and write $\partial_{j\alpha}=\partial/\partial x_{j\alpha}$. Set
\[
 G_j(w)=\sum_{\alpha=0}^2 e_\alpha\partial_{j\alpha}w,\qquad

levels.title: Regularized current and fiber potential

levels.component_tex:
Let $z=(T,\tau_1,\tau_2)$ vary in an open set $U\subset\mathbb R^3$. For $n\ge1$ let the spatial variables $\zeta$ range in a flat $n$-dimensional torus times an auxiliary open set in $\mathbb R^{2n}$. Let
$\Omega=\{(z,\zeta):z\in U,\ r(z,\zeta)<0\}$ have lateral wall $r=0$, where $r$ is a smooth real function on a neighborhood of the closure relative to $U$. Write $\Omega_z=\{\zeta:r(z,\zeta)<0\}$. Assume the closed fibers over each compact subset of $U$ form a compact set and that the spatial gradient $\nabla_\zeta r$ is nonzero on the wall.

Index the triples by $a\in\{T,1,\ldots,n\}$, so that $(x_{T0},x_{T1},x_{T2})=(T,\tau_1,\tau_2)$. For $1\le a\le n$ use the orthonormal flat torus directions in slot $0$ and the auxiliary coordinate pairs in slots $1$ and $2$. Write $\partial_{a\alpha}=\partial/\partial x_{a\alpha}$ for $\alpha\in\{0,1,2\}$. Use the real associative quaternion algebra $\mathbb H$ with unit $1$, basis $(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k)$, and multiplication
\[
 \mathbf i^2=\mathbf j^2=\mathbf k^2=-1,\qquad
 \mathbf i\mathbf j=\mathbf k,\quad
 \mathbf j\mathbf k=\mathbf i,\quad
 \mathbf k\mathbf i=\mathbf j .
\]
Reversing the order of distinct imaginary units changes the sign. Quaternion conjugation $q\mapsto\bar q$ fixes the real coefficient $\operatorname{Re}q$ and negates the three imaginary coefficients. The notation $^*$ denotes conjugate transpose.

Let $M=(M_{ab})_{a,b\in\{T,1,\ldots,n\}}$ be a smooth quaternionic matrix field up to the wall, with $M=M^*$. Thus $M_{TT}$ is the diagonal entry for the time triple. For $(e_0,e_1,e_2)=(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j)$ and smooth real $w$, define the column $G(w)$, the matrix $H(w)$, and the real tensor $M^{\mathbb R}$ by
\[
G_a(w)=\sum_{\alpha=0}^2e_\alpha\partial_{a\alpha}w,\quad
H_{ab}(w)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta=0}^2e_\alpha\bar e_\beta\,\partial_{a\alpha}\partial_{b\beta}w,\quad
M^\mathbb R_{a\alpha,b\beta}=\operatorname{Re}(\bar e_\alpha M_{ab}e_\beta).
\]
Assume the real columns have zero divergence, so $\sum_{a,\alpha}\partial_{a\alpha}M^\mathbb R_{a\alpha,b\beta}=0$ for every $b,\beta$. Suppose $u$ is real and smooth up to the wall with $u=0$ there, and let $\rho$ be the smooth boundary value of $u/r$. With $\Delta_z$ the Euclidean Laplacian on $U$, for every $\eta\in C_c^\infty(U)$ one has
\[
 \int_\Omega u M_{TT}\Delta_z\eta\,dz\,d\zeta
 = \int_\Omega \eta\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(MH(u))\,dz\,d\zeta
 - \int_U \eta(z)\int_{\partial\Omega_z}\rho\,G(r)^*MG(r)
                 \frac{dS_{\rm fib}}{|\nabla_\zeta r|}\,dz .
\]
Here $dS_{\rm fib}$ is the Euclidean surface measure in the spatial fiber and $dz\,d\zeta$ is product volume.

levels.title: Green identity for a moving fiber

levels.component_tex:
Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-dirichlet} gives the smooth potential, $A:B=0$, and the positivity and conservation of $A$. The Schur formula of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2} gives
\[
 H(B_0+u)=\sigma_0 e_Te_T^*+\Sigma,\qquad
 \sigma_0=\ell-c^*D_u^{-1}c,\qquad \Sigma\ge0,\qquad
 \det H(B_0+u)=\lambda\mu\sigma_0
\]
with $e_T$ the first coordinate vector. Consequently
\[
 A:H(u)=A:\Sigma+\mu\sigma_0=A:\Sigma+\lambda^{-1}\det H(B_0+u).
\]
The scalar Schur complement isolates the time entry as in the real tensor estimate of Serre \cite{r-71}, Proposition 2.2. The segment integral $E_z$ will produce a Laplacian that cancels the signed full determinant.

Apply Lemma~\ref{ms:fiber-green} on the total domain of these fibers. The inverse chart of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1} gives compact closed fibers over compact parameter sets and a nonzero spatial gradient of $r$ on the wall. Write $\nu=G(r)/|\nabla r|$ for the encoded outward unit normal.

Take $M=A$ and reverse the sign for $X_0$. The regularizing cofactor has zero normal coefficient by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-dirichlet}, so the boundary term is the stated flux $\mathcal B(z)=\int\rho\,G(r)^*A_{\rm w}G(r)\delta(r)\,\mathrm d\zeta$. The interior identity gives
\[
 \Delta_z X_0(z)=\mathcal B(z)-\int_{\Omega_z} A:\Sigma\,\mathrm d\zeta
 -\lambda^{-1}\int_{\Omega_z}\det H(B_0+u)\,\mathrm d\zeta .
\]

For the second term of the energy take $M=C(H(B_0+\theta u))$, whose columns are conserved by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-3}. The product rule from Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-1} applied to $r\rho$ on the wall shows
\[
 H(B_0+\theta u)|_{\nu^\perp}=(B+\theta\rho H(r))|_{\nu^\perp},
\]
since the two cross terms have a factor $G(r)$ and vanish on compression. The null line of $H(r)$ belongs to $\nu^\perp\cap\ker B$ by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1}; hence this compression is singular. The cofactor restriction identity in Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2} gives $\nu^*M\nu=0$ without a sign assumption on $H(B_0+\theta u)$. The same identity for $e_T$ gives $M_{TT}=\det D_{\theta u}$. Integrating Green's formula in $\theta$ and dividing by $\lambda$ therefore yields
\[
 \Delta_z E_z(u)=\lambda^{-1}\int_{\Omega_z}\det H(B_0+u)\,\mathrm d\zeta .
\]
In fact $M:H(u)=\partial_\theta\det H(B_0+\theta u)$, and the lower endpoint contributes $\det B=0$ because $B$ has rank at most one by the same holomorphic Hessian formula. Summing the two Laplacian identities proves the balance in distributions. The fiber chart identifies both volume and wall integrals smoothly with integrals on fixed domains, so the identities hold pointwise. Positivity of $A$ and $\Sigma$ gives $A:\Sigma\ge0$.

In the chosen frame $X=(x,b)$, assume the supported frequencies have $\kappa=(\xi_b+|\xi|)/\sqrt2>0$ and $|v|\le\gamma<w_0/4$, where $v=\xi_x/\kappa$. Set $y=|Y|$, $e=Y/y$, and $\iota_e(\alpha+\mathrm i\beta)=\alpha+e\mathbf i\beta$ for real $\alpha,\beta$. To obtain the wave current, form the following column in null coordinates $t=(T+b)/\sqrt2$, $s_0=(b-T)/\sqrt2$:
\[
 \chi=\sum_{\xi}
 \begin{pmatrix}1\\(v+W)/2\\-W\cdot v/2\end{pmatrix}
 \iota_e\!\bigl(\overline{\widehat f(\xi)e^{\mathrm i(X\cdot\xi-T|\xi|)}}\bigr)
 (\kappa/y)^{d/2}e^{-\kappa y|W-v|^2/2}.
\]
Use the orthogonal change of index from $(t,x,s_0)$ to $(T,x,b)$ to express $\chi$ in physical coordinates and set $A^0=\chi\chi^*$ there. For $\ell>0$ let $J_\ell$ be the periodization of the probability kernel $c_n\ell^{-n}(1+|X/\ell|^2)^{-n-2}$, with $c_n$ normalizing the integral. Fix a smooth $0\le g\le1$ on $\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}$ equal to one on $|Q|\le1/100$ and zero on $|Q|\ge1/20$. Define
\[
 A_{\rm w}=g(Q)(J_h*_X A^0),\qquad A=A_{\rm w}+h^{50n}C(H(r)),\qquad
 \mu=A_{TT},\qquad B_0=\lambda|\Phi|^2,\qquad\lambda=h^{-30n}.
\]
Here $*_X$ denotes convolution in the real periodic variables only. Put $B=H(B_0)$ and $B_{\rm fib}=H_{\rm fib}(B_0)$.

For sufficiently small $h>0$ with $4a\le1$, take the zero-boundary Dirichlet solution $u$ with $D_u>0$ and $\det D_u=\lambda\mu$, where $D_v=H_{\rm fib}(B_0+v)$. Write $\mathrm d\zeta=\mathrm dX\,\mathrm dP\,\mathrm dZ$,
\[
 X_0(z)=\int_{\Omega_z}(-u)\mu\,\mathrm d\zeta,\qquad
 E_z(v)=\lambda^{-1}\int_{\Omega_z}v\int_0^1\det D_{\theta v}\,\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\zeta,\qquad
 \mathcal F(z)=E_z(u)+X_0(z).
\]
If $H(B_0+u)=\begin{pmatrix}\ell&c^*\\c&D_u\end{pmatrix}$, put
$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}c^*D_u^{-1}c&c^*\\c&D_u\end{pmatrix}$.

\[

 =\int \rho\, G(r)^*A_{\rm w}G(r)\,\delta(r)\,\mathrm d\zeta .
\]
Here $A:\Sigma=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A\Sigma)$, $\Delta_z$ is the Laplacian in the three real coordinates of $z$, $G(r)$ is the full gradient, and $\delta(r)\,\mathrm d\zeta=\mathrm dS_{\rm fib}/|\nabla_{\rm fib}r|$ on the fixed fiber wall. In particular the right-hand side is an upper bound on $\Delta_z\mathcal F$.
levels.text:
Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-dirichlet} gives the smooth potential, $A:B=0$, and the positivity and conservation of $A$. The Schur formula of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2} gives
\[
 H(B_0+u)=\sigma_0 e_Te_T^*+\Sigma,\qquad
 \sigma_0=\ell-c^*D_u^{-1}c,\qquad \Sigma\ge0,\qquad
 \det H(B_0+u)=\lambda\mu\sigma_0
\]
with $e_T$ the first coordinate vector. Consequently
\[
 A:H(u)=A:\Sigma+\mu\sigma_0=A:\Sigma+\lambda^{-1}\det H(B_0+u).
\]
The scalar Schur complement isolates the time entry as in the real tensor estimate of Serre \cite{r-71}, Proposition 2.2. The segment integral $E_z$ will produce a Laplacian that cancels the signed full determinant.

Apply Lemma~\ref{ms:fiber-green} on the total domain of these fibers. The inverse chart of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1} gives compact closed fibers over compact parameter sets and a nonzero spatial gradient of $r$ on the wall. Write $\nu=G(r)/|\nabla r|$ for the encoded outward unit normal.

Take $M=A$ and reverse the sign for $X_0$. The regularizing cofactor has zero normal coefficient by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-dirichlet}, so the boundary term is the stated flux $\mathcal B(z)=\int\rho\,G(r)^*A_{\rm w}G(r)\delta(r)\,\mathrm d\zeta$. The interior identity gives
\[
 \Delta_z X_0(z)=\mathcal B(z)-\int_{\Omega_z} A:\Sigma\,\mathrm d\zeta
 -\lambda^{-1}\int_{\Omega_z}\det H(B_0+u)\,\mathrm d\zeta .
\]

For the second term of the energy take $M=C(H(B_0+\theta u))$, whose columns are conserved by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-3}. The product rule from Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-1} applied to $r\rho$ on the wall shows
\[
 H(B_0+\theta u)|_{\nu^\perp}=(B+\theta\rho H(r))|_{\nu^\perp},
\]
since the two cross terms have a factor $G(r)$ and vanish on compression. The null line of $H(r)$ belongs to $\nu^\perp\cap\ker B$ by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1}; hence this compression is singular. The cofactor restriction identity in Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2} gives $\nu^*M\nu=0$ without a sign assumption on $H(B_0+\theta u)$. The same identity for $e_T$ gives $M_{TT}=\det D_{\theta u}$. Integrating Green's formula in $\theta$ and dividing by $\lambda$ therefore yields
\[
 \Delta_z E_z(u)=\lambda^{-1}\int_{\Omega_z}\det H(B_0+u)\,\mathrm d\zeta .
\]
In fact $M:H(u)=\partial_\theta\det H(B_0+\theta u)$, and the lower endpoint contributes $\det B=0$ because $B$ has rank at most one by the same holomorphic Hessian formula. Summing the two Laplacian identities proves the balance in distributions. The fiber chart identifies both volume and wall integrals smoothly with integrals on fixed domains, so the identities hold pointwise. Positivity of $A$ and $\Sigma$ gives $A:\Sigma\ge0$.
