For $m=1$ the cofactor is identically one. Otherwise let $j_0=m-1$. By Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2}, $C$ is homogeneous of degree $j_0$. Polarize it by taking $Q(M_1,\ldots,M_{j_0})$ to be the coefficient of $t_1\cdots t_{j_0}$ in $C(\sum_jt_jM_j)$. This is multilinear and equals $j_0!C(M)$ on the diagonal $M_1=\cdots=M_{j_0}=M$.

Take $M_j=g_jg_j^*$ for quaternionic columns $g_j$. If all $t_j>0$, the kernel of $\sum_jt_jg_jg_j^*$ is the orthogonal complement of the span of the $g_j$, as seen by setting its nonnegative quadratic form equal to zero. Its image is that span, of dimension at most $m-1$. Its cofactor therefore kills every $g_j$ by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2}. The equalities are polynomial in $t$, so the coefficient $Q(g_1g_1^*,\ldots,g_{j_0}g_{j_0}^*)$ also kills every $g_j$. This coefficient is Hermitian, so $g_j^*Q=0$ as well.

Evaluate the polarized row divergence on $u_j(z)=\exp(\xi_j\cdot z)$ with arbitrary real covectors $\xi_j$ and the real coordinate dot product. Write $(g_j)_a=\sum_\alpha e_\alpha(\xi_j)_{a\alpha}$. The Hessian symbol in Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-1} gives
\[
Q(H(u_1),\ldots,H(u_{j_0}))
=e^{(\sum_j\xi_j)\cdot z}Q(g_1g_1^*,\ldots,g_{j_0}g_{j_0}^*).
\]
After dividing by the exponential, the row divergence is $(\sum_jg_j)^*Q=0$. On general smooth inputs this row divergence is a multilinear constant-coefficient differential expression. Its exponential test divided by the product of the exponentials is the polynomial whose monomials in the $\xi_j$ encode the derivatives of the respective inputs. It vanishes for all real covectors, so all its coefficients vanish. Taking every input equal to $u$ and dividing by $j_0!$ gives the assertion.

\[

\qquad(1\le b\le m).
\]

levels.component_tex:
By Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-2-2}, $A^0$ is positive semidefinite, has divergence-free real columns and satisfies $(\partial\Phi)A^0=0$. The holomorphic Hessian and gradient identities in Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-1} show that the images of $H(|\Phi|^2)$ and $G(g(Q))$ are contained in the quaternionic span of $(\partial\Phi)^*$. The averaged current still annihilates this span because $(\partial\Phi)^*$ is independent of $X$. Averaging preserves positivity and conservation. Multiplication by $g(Q)$ preserves positivity and adds only the term given by contraction with $G(g(Q))$ in the real column divergence, which vanishes. In particular $A_{\rm w}:H(|\Phi|^2)=0$.

By Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1}, the null line of $H(r)$ is orthogonal to $G(r)$ and lies in $\ker H(|\Phi|^2)$. The cofactor has image in this line, is positive semidefinite, and has time entry $\det H_{\rm fib}(r)>0$ by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2}. Its real columns have zero divergence by Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-3}. This proves the matrix claims and $\mu>0$, and the spatial eigenvalue claim follows from Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-4-1}.

For the density ceiling, apply Lemma~\ref{ms:wave-cap-estimates} to the annular cap. It gives $\kappa\asymp h^{-1}$ and $\sum_\xi |\widehat f(\xi)|\lesssim h^{-n/2}$. The weight in Proposition~\ref{ms:prop-2-2} is bounded by $(\kappa/|Y|)^{d/2}\lesssim h^{-d}$ because $|Y|\asymp s>a\ge h$, and its polarization columns are bounded on these fibers. The parametrization by the fixed ellipsoid gives the smooth family of domains. The theorem gives existence, uniqueness, smoothness in the parameters, and $u\le0$ by its barriers. Finally the eigenvalues of $B_{\rm fib}+\alpha I$ are $\beta+\alpha$ and $d$ copies of $\alpha$, giving the stated determinant.

\]

\[

levels.section_title: Green identity for a moving fiber: Proof of Lemma fiber-green
levels.statement:
Let $z=(T,\tau_1,\tau_2)$ vary in an open set $U\subset\mathbb R^3$. For $n\ge1$ let the spatial variables $\zeta$ range in a flat $n$-dimensional torus times an auxiliary open set in $\mathbb R^{2n}$. Let
$\Omega=\{(z,\zeta):z\in U,\ r(z,\zeta)<0\}$ have lateral wall $r=0$, where $r$ is a smooth real function on a neighborhood of the closure relative to $U$. Write $\Omega_z=\{\zeta:r(z,\zeta)<0\}$. Assume the closed fibers over each compact subset of $U$ form a compact set and that the spatial gradient $\nabla_\zeta r$ is nonzero on the wall.

Index the triples by $a\in\{T,1,\ldots,n\}$, so that $(x_{T0},x_{T1},x_{T2})=(T,\tau_1,\tau_2)$. For $1\le a\le n$ use the orthonormal flat torus directions in slot $0$ and the auxiliary coordinate pairs in slots $1$ and $2$. Write $\partial_{a\alpha}=\partial/\partial x_{a\alpha}$ for $\alpha\in\{0,1,2\}$. Use the real associative quaternion algebra $\mathbb H$ with unit $1$, basis $(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k)$, and multiplication
\[
 \mathbf i^2=\mathbf j^2=\mathbf k^2=-1,\qquad
 \mathbf i\mathbf j=\mathbf k,\quad
 \mathbf j\mathbf k=\mathbf i,\quad
 \mathbf k\mathbf i=\mathbf j .
\]
Reversing the order of distinct imaginary units changes the sign. Quaternion conjugation $q\mapsto\bar q$ fixes the real coefficient $\operatorname{Re}q$ and negates the three imaginary coefficients. The notation $^*$ denotes conjugate transpose.

Let $M=(M_{ab})_{a,b\in\{T,1,\ldots,n\}}$ be a smooth quaternionic matrix field up to the wall, with $M=M^*$. Thus $M_{TT}$ is the diagonal entry for the time triple. For $(e_0,e_1,e_2)=(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j)$ and smooth real $w$, define the column $G(w)$, the matrix $H(w)$, and the real tensor $M^{\mathbb R}$ by
\[
G_a(w)=\sum_{\alpha=0}^2e_\alpha\partial_{a\alpha}w,\quad
H_{ab}(w)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta=0}^2e_\alpha\bar e_\beta\,\partial_{a\alpha}\partial_{b\beta}w,\quad
M^\mathbb R_{a\alpha,b\beta}=\operatorname{Re}(\bar e_\alpha M_{ab}e_\beta).
\]
Assume the real columns have zero divergence, so $\sum_{a,\alpha}\partial_{a\alpha}M^\mathbb R_{a\alpha,b\beta}=0$ for every $b,\beta$. Suppose $u$ is real and smooth up to the wall with $u=0$ there, and let $\rho$ be the smooth boundary value of $u/r$. With $\Delta_z$ the Euclidean Laplacian on $U$, for every $\eta\in C_c^\infty(U)$ one has
\[
 \int_\Omega u M_{TT}\Delta_z\eta\,dz\,d\zeta
 = \int_\Omega \eta\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(MH(u))\,dz\,d\zeta
 - \int_U \eta(z)\int_{\partial\Omega_z}\rho\,G(r)^*MG(r)
                 \frac{dS_{\rm fib}}{|\nabla_\zeta r|}\,dz .
\]
Here $dS_{\rm fib}$ is the Euclidean surface measure in the spatial fiber and $dz\,d\zeta$ is product volume.

levels.component_tex:
By the rank-one determinant identity of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2},
\[
 \det D_{\theta u}
 =\theta^n\det D_u+(1-\theta)\theta^{n-1}C(D_u):B_{\rm fib}.
\]
Put $I=\int_{\Omega_z}(-u)C(D_u):B_{\rm fib}\,\mathrm d\zeta\ge0$. Integrating that polynomial in $\theta$ gives $\mathcal F=nX_0/(n+1)-I/[\lambda n(n+1)]$ and hence the upper bound. Homogeneity gives $C(D_u):D_u=n\det D_u$; therefore
\[
 n\lambda X_0-I=\int_{\Omega_z}(-u)C(D_u):H_{\rm fib}(u)\,\mathrm d\zeta
 =\int_{\Omega_z}G_{\rm fib}(u)^*C(D_u)G_{\rm fib}(u)\,\mathrm d\zeta.
\]

levels.section_title: Energy comparison: Proof of Lemma lemma-4-3
levels.statement:
Let $\mathbb H$ be the real associative algebra with basis $(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k)$, unit $1$, and multiplication determined by
$\mathbf i^2=\mathbf j^2=\mathbf k^2=-1$, $\mathbf i\mathbf j=\mathbf k$, $\mathbf j\mathbf k=\mathbf i$, and $\mathbf k\mathbf i=\mathbf j$, with the opposite products having the opposite signs. Quaternionic conjugation is
$\overline{q_0+q_1\mathbf i+q_2\mathbf j+q_3\mathbf k}=q_0-q_1\mathbf i-q_2\mathbf j-q_3\mathbf k$.
Write $\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}=\{x+\mathbf k y:x,y\in\mathbb R\}$ for the complex subalgebra with the inherited multiplication and conjugation. We use quaternionic columns with scalars acting on the right, and $A^*$ denotes quaternionic conjugate transpose.

Fix an integer $n\ge2$, a real parameter $a>0$, and $z=(T,\tau)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}$ with $a<|\tau|<4$. Let $\Omega_z=(\mathbb R^n/(100\mathbb Z^n))\times V_z$, where $V_z$ is the open set of $(P,Z)\in\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}^{n-1}\times\mathbb C_{\mathbf k}$ for which
\[
 Y=(\tau+Z)/\sqrt2\ne0,\qquad
 100\left|P/Y\right|^2+100\left|\frac{(Z-\tau)/\sqrt2+P\cdot P/(2Y)}{a}\right|^2<1,
\]
with $P\cdot P$ using the bilinear dot product. Write $x_{j0}$ for the spatial torus coordinates and $x_{j1}+\mathbf k x_{j2}$ for the components of $(P,Z)$ in matching order. With $(e_0,e_1,e_2)=(1,\mathbf i,\mathbf j)$ and $\partial_{j\alpha}=\partial/\partial x_{j\alpha}$, put
\[
G_{{\rm fib},j}(v)=\sum_{\alpha=0}^2e_\alpha\partial_{j\alpha}v,\qquad
H_{{\rm fib},jk}(v)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta=0}^2 e_\alpha\bar e_\beta
      \partial_{j\alpha}\partial_{k\beta}v .
\]
Use the Moore determinant on Hermitian quaternionic matrices. Its cofactor is defined by
$\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(C(D)B)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\det(D+tB)\right|_{t=0}$
for Hermitian $B$. Let $B_0\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega_z;\mathbb R)$ have positive semidefinite spatial quaternionic Hessian $B_{\rm fib}=H_{\rm fib}(B_0)$ of rank one. Let $\lambda>0$ be a constant and $\mu:\overline\Omega_z\to(0,\infty)$ the smooth Dirichlet density. Let $u\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega_z;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $u\le0$, $u|_{\partial\Omega_z}=0$, $D_u>0$ in $\Omega_z$, and $\det D_u=\lambda\mu$, where $D_v=H_{\rm fib}(B_0+v)$. Set
\[
 \mathcal F=\lambda^{-1}\int_{\Omega_z}u\int_0^1\det D_{\theta u}\,\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\zeta
  -\int_{\Omega_z}u\mu\,\mathrm d\zeta,
 \qquad X_0=\int_{\Omega_z}(-u)\mu\,\mathrm d\zeta.
\]
Then
\[
 \mathcal F=\frac{n-1}{n+1}X_0+\frac{1}{\lambda n(n+1)}
 \int_{\Omega_z} G_{\rm fib}(u)^* C(D_u)G_{\rm fib}(u)\,\mathrm d\zeta,
 \qquad
 \frac{n-1}{n+1}X_0\le\mathcal F\le\frac n{n+1}X_0.
\]
Here $\mathrm d\zeta=\mathrm dX\,\mathrm dP\,\mathrm dZ$ is ordinary fiber volume.
levels.text:
By the rank-one determinant identity of Lemma~\ref{ms:lemma-3-2},
\[

 =\theta^n\det D_u+(1-\theta)\theta^{n-1}C(D_u):B_{\rm fib}.
\]
Put $I=\int_{\Omega_z}(-u)C(D_u):B_{\rm fib}\,\mathrm d\zeta\ge0$. Integrating that polynomial in $\theta$ gives $\mathcal F=nX_0/(n+1)-I/[\lambda n(n+1)]$ and hence the upper bound. Homogeneity gives $C(D_u):D_u=n\det D_u$; therefore
\[
 n\lambda X_0-I=\int_{\Omega_z}(-u)C(D_u):H_{\rm fib}(u)\,\mathrm d\zeta
 =\int_{\Omega_z}G_{\rm fib}(u)^*C(D_u)G_{\rm fib}(u)\,\mathrm d\zeta.
\]

Rotation averaging yields
\((-\Delta_{T,\tau}+V(|\tau|))H(T,|\tau|)\ge0\).
We first bound the radial comparison solutions. For \(S=1\) or \(3\)
and fixed \(\kappa>0\), solve
\[
 u''+s^{-1}u'=(V+\kappa^2)u,\qquad b<s<S,
\]
with endpoint values \(0,1\) in either order.
Set \(x=\log(s/b)\), \(A=\log(S/b)\), and
\(P(x)=s^2(V(s)+\kappa^2)\). The equation in \(x\) is \(u_{xx}=Pu\).
Its solution \(\psi\) with \(\psi(0)=0\) and \(\psi'(0)=1\)
satisfies \(\psi(x)\ge x\): it begins positive, then has
\(\psi''\ge0\) wherever it is nonnegative. Integration gives
\[
 \frac{\psi(x)}x=1+\int_0^x \frac{z(x-z)}x
                  P(z)\frac{\psi(z)}z\,dz .
\]
For \(0\le z\le x\le A\) the coefficient \(z(x-z)/x\) is at most
\(\min(z,A-z)\). Gronwall's inequality therefore bounds
\(\psi(A)/A\) above by
\(\exp(\int_0^A\min(z,A-z)P(z)\,dz)\).
The part from \(V\) is at most
\(\int_b^S s\log(s/b)V(s)\,ds\le M\).
Writing \(t=A-z\), the part from \(\kappa^2\) is at most
\(\kappa^2S^2\int_0^\infty t e^{-2t}\,dt\).
Consequently the solution with values \(0,1\) is
\(\psi(x)/\psi(A)\ge c x/A\). Reflection \(x\mapsto A-x\)
preserves the weighted integral used in Gronwall's inequality
and yields \(u\ge c(1-x/A)\) for values \(1,0\).

Put \(m(s)=\int_0^3\sin(\pi T/3)H(T,s)\,dT\).
Integration by parts twice gives
\[
 \int_0^3\sin(\pi T/3)\,\partial_T^2H(T,s)\,dT
   =-(\pi/3)^2m(s)+(\pi/3)\big(H(0,s)+H(3,s)\big).
\]
The boundary term is nonnegative, so the supersolution inequality
implies \(m''+s^{-1}m'\le(V+\pi^2/9)m\).
Since \(m(3)\ge0\), the maximum principle and the radial
comparison with \(S=3\), \(\kappa=\pi/3\), and boundary values
\(1,0\) give \(m(s)\ge c(M)m(b)\log(3/s)/D\). In particular
\[
 \int_0^3\int_{3/4\le|\tau|\le5/4}H(T,|\tau|)\,d\tau\,dT
 \ge c(M)m(b)/D.
\]

We transfer this integrated bound to \(H(T,1)\) for \(|T|\le1\).
On \(-2<T<4,\ 1/2<|\tau|<3/2\) one has \(\Delta H\le MH\).
Write \(x=(T,\tau)\). The function
\(H(x)\cos(\sqrt{M+1}\,v)\) in the additional real variable \(v\)
is nonnegative and superharmonic on a fixed small slab about
\(v=0\). The mean inequality on the four-dimensional ball of
radius \(2\rho\) about \((x,0)\), restricted to
\(B_\rho(x)\times[-\rho,\rho]\), gives
\[
 H(x)\ge c\rho^{-3}\int_{B_\rho(x)} H(y)\,dy
\]
for one sufficiently small \(\rho>0\), uniformly on a neighborhood
of the compact connected band
\([-1,3]\times\{3/4\le|\tau|\le5/4\}\).
Let \(B_1,\ldots,B_N\) be a finite cover of the band by balls of
radius \(\rho/4\) centered in the band. The overlap graph is
connected because each ball meets the band and the band is
connected. The integrated bound gives one ball \(B_{j_0}\) with
mass \(I_{j_0}=\int_{B_{j_0}}H\ge c(M)m(b)/(ND)\).
For any overlapping pair \(B_i,B_j\), every \(x\in B_j\) has
\(B_i\subset B_\rho(x)\). Nonnegativity and the mean inequality
therefore give \(\inf_{B_j}H\ge c\rho^{-3}I_i\). Integrating on
\(B_j\) gives \(I_j\ge c\rho^{-3}|B_j|I_i\), with a fixed
positive factor because \(|B_j|\) is proportional to \(\rho^3\).
Thus along a chain from \(B_{j_0}\) the lower mass bound passes
from each known ball to the next one. A shortest chain has at
most \(N-1\) edges. Applying the mean inequality within each
ball to its resulting mass gives \(\inf_{B_j}H\ge c(M)m(b)/D\)
for every \(j\). In particular this holds at \((T,\tau)\) with
\(|T|\le1\) and \(|\tau|=1\).

For the return passage use the radial solution for
\(S=1\), \(\kappa=\pi/2\), \(u(b)=0\), \(u(1)=1\). On
\(|T|<1,\ b<|\tau|<1\), the function
\[
 w(T,\tau)=c(M)m(b)D^{-1}\cos(\pi T/2)\,u(|\tau|)
\]
solves \((-\Delta_{T,\tau}+V)w=0\).
It vanishes on \(|T|=1\) and \(|\tau|=b\); it is at most
\(H(T,1)\) on \(|\tau|=1\) for a sufficiently small \(c(M)\).
The maximum principle and the radial lower bound imply
\[

              \frac{\log(r/b)}{\log(1/b)}.
\]
Use \(\log(1/b)\le D\) and the positive lower bound for
\(\sin(\pi T/3)\) on \([1,2]\) to conclude.

levels.title: Propagation across a thin cylinder

levels.component_tex:
The low-frequency wave multiplier is smooth off the origin. The following multiplier bound controls it by derivative estimates there.

\begin{Proposition}[Mihlin--H\"ormander multiplier bound]\label{ext:mihlin-multiplier}
Let $n\ge1$, $N=\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1$ and $1<p<\infty$. For a complex symbol $m\in C^N(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})$ assume
\[
 A=\max_{|\alpha|\le N}\ \sup_{\xi\ne0}|\xi|^{|\alpha|}
             |\partial_\xi^\alpha m(\xi)|<\infty.
\]
For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ define $m(D)f=(m\widehat f)^\vee$ using
\[
 \widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-ix\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx,\qquad
 g^\vee(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{ix\cdot\xi}g(\xi)\,d\xi .
\]
The value of $m$ at the origin is immaterial. Then
\[
 \|m(D)f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}
 \le C_{n,p} A\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}
 \qquad (f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)).
\]
By density $m(D)$ extends uniquely to a bounded operator on $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfying the same inequality for every $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$.
Indeed the displayed derivative bounds imply the annular $L^2$ bounds
$\|\partial^\alpha m\|_{L^2(\{R<|\xi|<2R\})}\le C_n A R^{n/2-|\alpha|}$
used in \cite{r-32}, Theorem~6.2.7 and (6.2.14), p.~446.
\end{Proposition}

Let \(n\ge2\), \(d=n-1\), \(I=[1,2]\), and let
\(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})\).

\(\widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n} e^{-iX\cdot\xi}f(X)\,dX\)
with inverse factor \((2\pi)^{-n}\). For \(0<h\le1/2\) let
\(U(T)\) and \(P_h\) be the multipliers \(e^{-iT|\xi|}\) and
\(\varphi(h\xi)\), respectively. For \(2\le p\le\infty\), set

\[

 \le C_{n,p,\varphi}\,h^{-s_+(p)}[\log(2/h)]^{\beta(p)}
                 \|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)} .
\]

The low-frequency wave multiplier is smooth off the origin. The following multiplier bound controls it by derivative estimates there.

\begin{Proposition}[Mihlin--H\"ormander multiplier bound]\label{ext:mihlin-multiplier}
Let $n\ge1$, $N=\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1$ and $1<p<\infty$. For a complex symbol $m\in C^N(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})$ assume
\[
 A=\max_{|\alpha|\le N}\ \sup_{\xi\ne0}|\xi|^{|\alpha|}
             |\partial_\xi^\alpha m(\xi)|<\infty.
\]
For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ define $m(D)f=(m\widehat f)^\vee$ using
\[
 \widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-ix\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx,\qquad
 g^\vee(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{ix\cdot\xi}g(\xi)\,d\xi .
\]
The value of $m$ at the origin is immaterial. Then
\[
 \|m(D)f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}
 \le C_{n,p} A\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}
 \qquad (f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)).
\]
By density $m(D)$ extends uniquely to a bounded operator on $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfying the same inequality for every $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$.
Indeed the displayed derivative bounds imply the annular $L^2$ bounds
$\|\partial^\alpha m\|_{L^2(\{R<|\xi|<2R\})}\le C_n A R^{n/2-|\alpha|}$
used in \cite{r-32}, Theorem~6.2.7 and (6.2.14), p.~446.
\end{Proposition}

levels.component_tex:
Plancherel and \(|I|=1\) give the \(L^2(\mathbb R^n)\) to
\(L^2(I\times\mathbb R^n)\) norm bound \(\|\varphi\|_\infty\).
We next show an \(O(h^{-d/2})\) bound for \(p=\infty\).
Take a maximal \(c\sqrt h\)-separated net on \(S^{n-1}\) for
fixed small \(c>0\). Counting disjoint spherical balls of
half this radius bounds the number of centers by
\(O(h^{-d/2})\); the same volume comparison gives bounded
overlap of the caps of radius \(2c\sqrt h\).
A smooth partition on those caps is obtained from bumps in
\(|\omega-\omega_\nu|^2/h\), equal to one at distances at
most \(c\sqrt h\), by division by their sum. The denominator
is at least one. Multiply these cutoffs by \(\varphi(\eta)\).
In coordinates \(\eta=(\sqrt h\,z,\rho)\) with axis
\(\omega_\nu\), the resulting cutoff has fixed compact
support, with \(\rho\) bounded below. Its derivatives in
\((z,\rho)\) of any fixed order are uniformly bounded.
In fact each neighboring center has transverse coordinates
\(O(\sqrt h)\) and axial coordinate \(1+O(h)\) in this frame.
The transverse coordinates of \(\omega=\eta/|\eta|\)
are \(\sqrt h\,z/(\rho^2+h|z|^2)^{1/2}\), and
\((\omega\cdot\omega_\nu-1)/h\) is uniformly smooth on
this compact set after rationalizing the difference.
It follows that the arguments \(|\omega-\omega_\mu|^2/h\)
of the overlapping bumps have uniformly bounded derivatives.

Remove the linear phase \(T\rho/h\) from the multiplier phase.
The remaining phase factor is controlled by
\[
 \frac{T}{h}(\sqrt{\rho^2+h|z|^2}-\rho)
 =\frac{T|z|^2}{\sqrt{\rho^2+h|z|^2}+\rho}.
\]
It has uniformly bounded derivatives on the support for
\(T\in I\). Repeated integration by parts bounds the \(L^1\)
norm of the inverse Fourier transform in the rescaled
variables uniformly. Invertible linear frequency changes
preserve that kernel norm by the Jacobian, and multiplication
by the removed linear phase translates the kernel.
Thus every cap contributes \(O(1)\) to the spatial kernel
\(L^1\) norm. Their number proves the \(L^\infty\) endpoint
bound, uniformly in \(T\).

At \(p_c=2n/d\) use \ref{ms:thm-1-2}, with \(N=h^{-1}\) and
\(\log(2+N)\) comparable to \(\log(2/h)\).
Apply Riesz--Thorin to the linear operator
\(f\mapsto U(T)P_h f\) between the spatial and spacetime
Lebesgue spaces \cite{r-32}. For \(2\le p\le p_c\) the weight
of the critical estimate is
\[
 \frac{1/2-1/p}{1/2-1/p_c}=n(1-2/p),
\]
so the log exponent is \(d(1-2/p)\) with no power of \(h^{-1}\).
For \(p_c\le p\le\infty\) its weight is \(p_c/p\), giving
log exponent \(2/p\) and frequency exponent
\((d/2)(1-p_c/p)=d/2-n/p\). These are the stated exponents.

Let \(0<\delta\le1/2\), let \(\{\omega_j\}\subset S^{n-1}\) be \(\delta\)-separated, and let \(T_j\) be the open \(2\delta\)-neighborhood of \(x_j+[-1/2,1/2]\omega_j\) for arbitrary \(x_j\in\mathbb R^n\). For \(a_j\ge0\),
\[
 \left\|\sum_j a_j\mathbf1_{T_j}\right\|_{L^q(\mathbb R^n)}
 \lesssim L(1/\delta)^{2A}\left(\delta^d\sum_j a_j^q\right)^{1/q}.
\]

levels.title: Tube overlap from local spherical extension

levels.component_tex:
Write \(d=n-1\), \(p=p_c\), \(q=p/2\), and \(L(R)=\log(2+R)\). The extension bound is for every \(g\in L^p(S^{n-1},d\sigma)\), and the tube bound is for every \(f\in L^n(\mathbb R^n)\); each bound is uniform over these inputs. Apply \ref{ms:thm-1-2} with a smooth radial annular cutoff equal to one near the unit sphere. Its power \(A=2/p\) in \ref{ms:lemma-9-2} gives the first bound.

For \(0<\delta\le1/2\), take a maximal \(\delta\)-separated set \(\{\omega_j\}\) in \(S^{n-1}\). Each average defining \(K_\delta f(\omega)\) is at most a constant times the corresponding \(2\delta\)-tube average in any direction \(\omega_j\) within \(\delta\) of \(\omega\). Indeed the first tube lies in the second, and each tube has volume comparable to \(\delta^d\). The averages are continuous in center and direction by continuity of translation and rotation of tube indicators in \(L^q\), so their supremum is measurable. The covering by caps of radius \(\delta\) gives
\[
 \|K_\delta f\|_{L^n(S^{n-1})}
 \lesssim\left(\delta^d\sum_j K_{2\delta}f(\omega_j)^n\right)^{1/n}.
\]
Test this discrete norm by \(a_j\ge0\) with \(\delta^d\sum_j a_j^q=1\). For any centers \(x_j\), put \(T_j=T_{2\delta}(\omega_j,x_j)\). Hölder's inequality and \ref{ms:lemma-9-4} give
\[
 \delta^d\sum_j \frac{a_j}{|T_j|}\int_{T_j}|f|
 \lesssim\int |f|\sum_j a_j\mathbf 1_{T_j}
 \lesssim L(1/\delta)^{2A}\|f\|_n.
\]
Take the suprema over centers and weights. For \(1/2\le\delta\le1\), Hölder's inequality on each tube gives the bound.

Let \(F\) contain a unit segment in every direction. Its open \(\delta\)-neighborhood contains the tubes around those segments, so \(1\lesssim L(1/\delta)^{2A}|F_\delta|^{1/n}\). To prove the Hausdorff assertion use ball covers, grouping radii as in \cite{r-44}, Claim 3.2. For a countable cover by balls \(B_j\) of radii \(r_j\le e^{-2^m}\), put
\[
 J_k=\{j:2^k\le\log(1/r_j)<2^{k+1}\},\quad
 \delta_k=e^{-2^{k+1}},\quad G_k=\bigcup_{j\in J_k}2B_j,\quad v_k=\sum_{j\in J_k}r_j^n.
\]
At a point on a given unit segment covered by a ball in \(J_k\), its transverse disk of radius \(\delta_k\) lies in that doubled ball. Disks at different points form disjoint cross-sections of the tube. Hence the length covered by group \(k\) is at most a dimensional constant times \(K_{\delta_k}\mathbf1_{G_k}\) in the direction of the segment. All groups together cover length one in every direction. The triangle inequality, the maximal estimate, and Hölder in \(k\) give for any \(\gamma>n-1\)
\[
 1\lesssim \sum_{k\ge m}2^{2Ak}v_k^{1/n}
 \lesssim \left(\sum_j h_\gamma(r_j)\right)^{1/n}
 \left(\sum_{k\ge m}k^{-\gamma/(n-1)}\right)^{(n-1)/n},
\quad h_\gamma(r)=r^n[\log(1/r)]^{2An}[\log\log(1/r)]^\gamma .
\]
The last factor tends to zero. The gauge is doubling for small radii, so the ball covers give infinite Hausdorff measure for \(h_\gamma\). Since \(h_\gamma(r)=o(r^s)\) for every \(s<n\), the dimension is \(n\).

levels.statement:
Let \(n\ge2\), \(p_c=2n/(n-1)\), and let \(d\sigma\) be surface measure on \(S^{n-1}\). Write
\[
 Eg(X)=\int_{S^{n-1}} e^{iX\cdot\omega}g(\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega).
\]
Let \(T_\delta(\omega,x)\) be the open \(\delta\)-neighborhood of \(x+[-1/2,1/2]\omega\). Define \(K_\delta f(\omega)\) as the supremum over \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) of the average of \(|f|\) over \(T_\delta(\omega,x)\). For \(R\ge2\), \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(0<\delta\le1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|Eg\|_{L^{p_c}(B(z,R))}&\le C_n[\log(2+R)]^{2/p_c}\|g\|_{L^{p_c}(S^{n-1})},\\
 \|K_\delta f\|_{L^n(S^{n-1})}&\le C_n[\log(2/\delta)]^{4/p_c}\|f\|_{L^n(\mathbb R^n)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every subset of \(\mathbb R^n\) containing a unit line segment in each direction has Hausdorff dimension \(n\).
levels.text:
Write \(d=n-1\), \(p=p_c\), \(q=p/2\), and \(L(R)=\log(2+R)\). The extension bound is for every \(g\in L^p(S^{n-1},d\sigma)\), and the tube bound is for every \(f\in L^n(\mathbb R^n)\); each bound is uniform over these inputs. Apply \ref{ms:thm-1-2} with a smooth radial annular cutoff equal to one near the unit sphere. Its power \(A=2/p\) in \ref{ms:lemma-9-2} gives the first bound.

For \(0<\delta\le1/2\), take a maximal \(\delta\)-separated set \(\{\omega_j\}\) in \(S^{n-1}\). Each average defining \(K_\delta f(\omega)\) is at most a constant times the corresponding \(2\delta\)-tube average in any direction \(\omega_j\) within \(\delta\) of \(\omega\). Indeed the first tube lies in the second, and each tube has volume comparable to \(\delta^d\). The averages are continuous in center and direction by continuity of translation and rotation of tube indicators in \(L^q\), so their supremum is measurable. The covering by caps of radius \(\delta\) gives
\[
 \|K_\delta f\|_{L^n(S^{n-1})}
 \lesssim\left(\delta^d\sum_j K_{2\delta}f(\omega_j)^n\right)^{1/n}.
\]
Test this discrete norm by \(a_j\ge0\) with \(\delta^d\sum_j a_j^q=1\). For any centers \(x_j\), put \(T_j=T_{2\delta}(\omega_j,x_j)\). Hölder's inequality and \ref{ms:lemma-9-4} give
\[
 \delta^d\sum_j \frac{a_j}{|T_j|}\int_{T_j}|f|
 \lesssim\int |f|\sum_j a_j\mathbf 1_{T_j}
 \lesssim L(1/\delta)^{2A}\|f\|_n.
\]
Take the suprema over centers and weights. For \(1/2\le\delta\le1\), Hölder's inequality on each tube gives the bound.

Let \(F\) contain a unit segment in every direction. Its open \(\delta\)-neighborhood contains the tubes around those segments, so \(1\lesssim L(1/\delta)^{2A}|F_\delta|^{1/n}\). To prove the Hausdorff assertion use ball covers, grouping radii as in \cite{r-44}, Claim 3.2. For a countable cover by balls \(B_j\) of radii \(r_j\le e^{-2^m}\), put
\[
 J_k=\{j:2^k\le\log(1/r_j)<2^{k+1}\},\quad
 \delta_k=e^{-2^{k+1}},\quad G_k=\bigcup_{j\in J_k}2B_j,\quad v_k=\sum_{j\in J_k}r_j^n.
\]
At a point on a given unit segment covered by a ball in \(J_k\), its transverse disk of radius \(\delta_k\) lies in that doubled ball. Disks at different points form disjoint cross-sections of the tube. Hence the length covered by group \(k\) is at most a dimensional constant times \(K_{\delta_k}\mathbf1_{G_k}\) in the direction of the segment. All groups together cover length one in every direction. The triangle inequality, the maximal estimate, and Hölder in \(k\) give for any \(\gamma>n-1\)
\[
 1\lesssim \sum_{k\ge m}2^{2Ak}v_k^{1/n}
 \lesssim \left(\sum_j h_\gamma(r_j)\right)^{1/n}
 \left(\sum_{k\ge m}k^{-\gamma/(n-1)}\right)^{(n-1)/n},
\quad h_\gamma(r)=r^n[\log(1/r)]^{2An}[\log\log(1/r)]^\gamma .
\]
The last factor tends to zero. The gauge is doubling for small radii, so the ball covers give infinite Hausdorff measure for \(h_\gamma\). Since \(h_\gamma(r)=o(r^s)\) for every \(s<n\), the dimension is \(n\).
levels.title: Spherical extension and Kakeya

levels.component_tex:
Put \(d=n-1\), \(L(R)=\log(2+R)\), and choose a nonzero, nonnegative \(\psi\in C_c^\infty((1,2))\). Define
\[
 M_N f=\int\psi(T)e^{iNT}U(T)\chi(|D|/N)f\,dT .
\]
Hölder's inequality in \(T\) and the assumed estimate give \(\|M_N f\|_p\lesssim L(N)^A\|f\|_p\), with extension by density to \(L^p\). Its multiplier is \(\chi(\rho/N)\widehat\psi(\rho-N)\) at \(\rho=|\xi|\), where \(\widehat\psi(s)=\int e^{-iTs}\psi(T)\,dT\). For \(1/2\le |Z|\le3\), its kernel is
\[
 K_N(Z)=c_n N^{d/2}|Z|^{-d/2}e^{iN|Z|}\psi(|Z|)+O(N^{d/2-1}),\qquad c_n\ne0 .
\]
Indeed, in polar coordinates the angular integral at \(u=\rho|Z|\) has expansion
\[
 \int_{S^{n-1}}e^{iu\omega_1}\,d\sigma(\omega)
   =u^{-d/2}(c_+e^{iu}+c_-e^{-iu})+O(u^{-d/2-1})
\]
by stationary phase at its two poles, with \(c_+c_-\ne0\). The radial integral of the remainder is \(O(N^{d/2-1})\) by the annular support and integrability of \(\widehat\psi\). In each main term the prefactor \(\chi(\rho/N)\rho^{d/2}\), extended by zero to negative \(\rho\), equals \(N^{d/2}\) at \(N\) and has derivative \(O(N^{d/2-1})\). Replacing it by \(N^{d/2}\) in the integral over the real line costs \(O(N^{d/2-1})\) by the first absolute moment of \(\widehat\psi\). Fourier inversion then gives \(\psi(\pm|Z|)\), of which only the positive argument contributes.

Set \(f_N(r\omega)=e^{-iNr}\psi(r)g(\omega)\), so \(\|f_N\|_p=C_\psi\|g\|_p\). The following linearization follows the passage from oscillatory integrals to extension in \cite{r-38}, Section 3, equations (3.8)--(3.9). For \(|X|\le R\), \(N\ge4R\), and \(r\in\operatorname{supp}\psi\),
\[
 N|r\omega-X/N|=Nr-X\cdot\omega+O(R^2/N).
\]
In the convolution against \(f_N\), the radial phases cancel and the amplitude changes by \(O(R/N)\) relative to its value at \(r\). The kernel expansion therefore gives
\[
 N^{-d/2}M_N f_N(X/N)
  =c' Eg(-X)+O((1+R^2)N^{-1}\|g\|_1),\qquad
 c'=c_n\int r^{d/2}\psi(r)^2\,dr\ne0.
\]
Choose \(N=(4+R)^{3+n/p}\). The error in \(L^p(B(0,R))\) is \(O(\|g\|_p)\), using finite sphere measure. The change of variables \(X=NY\) gives the prefactor \(N^{n/p-d/2}=1\) in the norm of the left side, and \(L(N)\lesssim_n L(R)\). Modulating \(g(\omega)\) by \(e^{iz\cdot\omega}\) translates the estimate to the ball centered at \(z\).

\[

\[
 \|Eg\|_{L^p(B(z,R))}\lesssim [\log(2+R)]^A\|g\|_{L^p(S^{n-1})}.
\]

levels.title: Spherical extension from the critical wave estimate

levels.component_tex:
We use the sign averaging across a disjoint decomposition from Beckner, Carbery, Semmes and Soria \cite{r-7}, Lemma~1, alongside their cap estimate in Lemma~2 (p.~395). For a related cap decomposition and square-function argument, see Bourgain \cite{r-13}, Section~6, (6.32)--(6.41), pp.~179--181. For small fixed \(c>0\) take disjoint caps \(C_j=\{|\omega-\omega_j|<c\delta\}\) on the sphere and set \(h_j(\omega)=e^{-i\delta^{-2}x_j\cdot\omega}\mathbf1_{C_j}(\omega)\). On \(T_j\), write \(Y-x_j=t\omega_j+v\) with \(|t|\le1/2\), \(|v|<2\delta\). Since \(\omega_j\cdot(\omega-\omega_j)=-|\omega-\omega_j|^2/2\), the phase in \(Eh_j(\delta^{-2}Y)\) differs from its value at \(\omega_j\) by at most \(c^2/4+2c\). Thus \(|Eh_j(\delta^{-2}Y)|\gtrsim\delta^d\) there.

Group the centers by the half-open unit lattice cubes \(Q\), with \(J_Q=\{j:x_j\in Q\}\). All tubes from a group lie in \(5Q\), whose dilation by \(\delta^{-2}\) lies in a ball of radius \(C_n\delta^{-2}\). For independent symmetric signs \(\varepsilon_j\), set \(g_\varepsilon=\sum_{j\in J_Q}\varepsilon_j a_j^{1/2}h_j\). Its \(L^p\) norm to the \(p\)-th power is bounded by \(C\delta^d\sum_{j\in J_Q}a_j^q\) by disjointness. Jensen's inequality yields
\[
 \mathbb E|Eg_\varepsilon|^p\ge
 \left(\sum_{j\in J_Q}a_j|Eh_j|^2\right)^q .
\]
Integrate over \(\delta^{-2}(5Q)\), apply the assumed ball estimate on its enclosing ball, and change variables to \(Y\). This gives
\[
 \delta^{dp-2n}\int_{5Q}\left(\sum_{j\in J_Q}a_j\mathbf1_{T_j}\right)^q
 \lesssim L(1/\delta)^{Ap}\delta^d\sum_{j\in J_Q}a_j^q .
\]
Here \(dp=2n\). Bounded overlap of \(5Q\) bounds the \(q\)-th power of the desired norm by a constant times the sum of the group integrals. Take the \(q\)-th root and use \(Ap/q=2A\).
levels.section_title: Tube overlap from local spherical extension: Proof of Lemma lemma-9-4
levels.statement:

\[

\]

\[

 \lesssim L(1/\delta)^{2A}\left(\delta^d\sum_j a_j^q\right)^{1/q}.
\]

levels.component_tex: Let \(n\ge2\), \(2\le b<\infty\), and \(b'\le a\le\infty\). Let \(E\) denote extension with the phase \(x\cdot\omega\) and surface measure \(d\sigma\) on \(S^{n-1}\). Assume \(E:L^a(S^{n-1})\to L^b(\mathbb R^n)\) is bounded. Then extension \(E_\Sigma\) with phase \(x\cdot\xi+t\tau\) and induced surface measure on \(\Sigma=\{(\rho\omega,\rho):1\le\rho\le2,\ \omega\in S^{n-1}\}\) is bounded \(L^a(\Sigma)\to L^b(\mathbb R^{n+1})\).

levels.title: Slicing the truncated cone

levels.component_tex:
Let \(p_c=2n/(n-1)\). By \ref{ms:thm-1-2} and \ref{ms:lemma-9-2}, local spherical extension \(L^{p_c}(S^{n-1})\to L^{p_c}(B(0,R))\) has norm \(O([\log(2+R)]^{2/p_c})\), hence \(O_\epsilon(R^\epsilon)\) for each \(\epsilon>0\). Duality gives the same loss for restriction \(f\mapsto\widehat f|_{S^{n-1}}\) from \(L^{p_c'}(\mathbb R^n)\) for \(f\) supported in \(B(0,R)\), with values in \(L^{p_c'}(S^{n-1})\). Here \(\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-ix\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx\). Apply the epsilon-removal theorem of \cite{r-75}, Theorem 1.2. Its consequence used here is that local \(L^u\to L^u\) restriction on the sphere at every loss \(O_\epsilon(R^\epsilon)\), for \(1<u<2\), yields global \(L^v(\mathbb R^n)\to L^u(S^{n-1})\) bounds for each \(1<v<u\). Since \(p_c'\in(1,2)\), this gives global diagonal \(L^v\to L^v\) restriction by finite sphere measure, and therefore by duality spherical extension \(L^s\to L^s\) for every \(p_c<s<\infty\).

If \(a\ge b\), take \(s=b\) and use finite measure of the sphere. If \(a<b\), set \(s=1+b/a'\). The range hypotheses give \(p_c<s<b\). Interpolate the diagonal estimate and the defining integral bound \(E:L^1\to L^\infty\) with weight \(\theta=s/b\) on the diagonal estimate. The interpolated input and output reciprocals are \(1-\theta+\theta/s=1/a\) and \(\theta/s=1/b\), so the spherical estimate holds.

For finite \(b\) the hypotheses imply \(b>2\) and \(b>a'\), hence \(a>b'\). The spherical bound passes to the cone by \ref{ms:cone-slicing}. For \(b=\infty\) each defining integral is bounded by the \(L^1\) norm, which is bounded by the \(L^a\) norm on a compact surface.
levels.section_title: Global Fourier extension from the sphere and cone: Proof of Corollary cor-9-3
levels.statement:
Let \(n\ge2\), \(p_c=2n/(n-1)\), and write \(a'\) for the Hölder conjugate of \(a\). On \(S^{n-1}\) with surface measure \(d\sigma\), put \(Eg(x)=\int e^{ix\cdot\omega}g(\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega)\). On the truncated cone \(\Sigma=\{(\rho\omega,\rho):1\le\rho\le2,\ \omega\in S^{n-1}\}\) with induced surface measure \(d\Sigma\), put
\[
 E_\Sigma G(x,t)=\int_\Sigma e^{i(x\cdot\xi+t\tau)}G(\xi,\tau)\,d\Sigma(\xi,\tau).
\]
If \(1<a\le\infty\), \(b<\infty\), and \(b>p_c\) and \(b>(n+1)a'/(n-1)\), then the strong bounds
\[
 \|Eg\|_{L^b(\mathbb R^n)}\lesssim_{n,a,b}\|g\|_{L^a(S^{n-1})},\qquad
 \|E_\Sigma G\|_{L^b(\mathbb R^{n+1})}\lesssim_{n,a,b}\|G\|_{L^a(\Sigma)}
\]
hold. For \(b=\infty\) both bounds hold for every \(1\le a\le\infty\).

levels.title: Global Fourier extension from the sphere and cone

levels.component_tex:
Use slicing as in \cite{r-61}, Theorem 1.2(a)(i). Write \(G_\rho(\omega)=G(\rho\omega,\rho)\). The surface measure in these coordinates is \(\sqrt2\,\rho^{n-1}d\rho\,d\sigma(\omega)\). Thus
\[
 E_\Sigma G(x,t)=\sqrt2\int_1^2 e^{it\rho}\rho^{n-1}E(G_\rho)(\rho x)\,d\rho .
\]
Apply Hausdorff--Young in \(t\) and Minkowski in \(x,\rho\), using \(b\ge b'\). After spatial dilation \(\rho x\mapsto x\) this gives
\[
 \|E_\Sigma G\|_{L^b_{x,t}}\lesssim
 \left(\int_1^2\big[\rho^{n-1-n/b}\|E(G_\rho)\|_{L^b_x}\big]^{b'}\,d\rho\right)^{1/b'}
 \lesssim\big\|\|G_\rho\|_{L^a(S^{n-1})}\big\|_{L^{b'}([1,2])}.
\]
Since \(a\ge b'\) and \(\rho^{n-1}\) is comparable to \(1\) on this interval, the right side is bounded by a constant times \(\|G\|_{L^a(\Sigma)}\).

Assume \(E:L^a(S^{n-1})\to L^b(\mathbb R^n)\) is bounded. Then extension \(E_\Sigma\) with phase \(x\cdot\xi+t\tau\) and induced surface measure on \(\Sigma=\{(\rho\omega,\rho):1\le\rho\le2,\ \omega\in S^{n-1}\}\) is bounded \(L^a(\Sigma)\to L^b(\mathbb R^{n+1})\).

 E_\Sigma G(x,t)=\sqrt2\int_1^2 e^{it\rho}\rho^{n-1}E(G_\rho)(\rho x)\,d\rho .
\]
Apply Hausdorff--Young in \(t\) and Minkowski in \(x,\rho\), using \(b\ge b'\). After spatial dilation \(\rho x\mapsto x\) this gives
\[

 \lesssim\big\|\|G_\rho\|_{L^a(S^{n-1})}\big\|_{L^{b'}([1,2])}.
\]
Since \(a\ge b'\) and \(\rho^{n-1}\) is comparable to \(1\) on this interval, the right side is bounded by a constant times \(\|G\|_{L^a(\Sigma)}\).

levels.component_tex:
Put \(A=2/p_c\) and \(L(R)=\log(2+R)\). The Kakeya bound of \ref{ms:cor-9-1}, with power \(2A\), gives the bound \(C L(1/\rho)^{2A}\) in \ref{ms:nikodym-distal} for the supremum \(D_\rho\) over neighborhoods of the ray segments at distances between \(1/2\) and \(1\) from \(x\).

Take any unit segment through \(x\). Its points within \(2\delta\) of \(x\), with their \(\delta\)-neighborhood, lie in \(B(x,3\delta)\). On each of the two rays the rest lies in the union of the intervals of distances \([s/2,s]\) with \(s=2^{-j}\), \(j\ge0\), \(s\ge\delta\). For such \(s\), a \(\delta\)-neighborhood of the ray interval has volume \(\lesssim_n s\delta^{n-1}\), as \(\delta\le s\). The full tube volume is comparable to \(\delta^{n-1}\); thus the ball and ray intervals contribute at most a constant times \(\delta\) and \(s\), respectively, times their individual maximal averages. The ball average has \(L^n\) operator norm one by Young's inequality. The maximal ray average at scale \(s\) is conjugate by dilation to \(D_{\delta/s}\), so its norm is bounded by \(C L(s/\delta)^{2A}\). Consequently
\[
 \|N_\delta\|_{L^n\to L^n}
 \lesssim \delta+\sum_{\substack{s=2^{-j},\ j\ge0\\ s\ge\delta}}sL(s/\delta)^{2A}
 \lesssim L(1/\delta)^{2A}.
\]

levels.component_tex:
We use the projective change of variables from \cite{r-75}, Theorem 4.10, and \cite{r-30}, Section 2.2. A finite set of rotations reduces the direction supremum to \(|\omega_n|\ge c_n\) for some \(c_n>0\). Translate any unit cube \(Q\) to the origin and write \(x=(x',t_0)\in Q\). For \(\rho\) sufficiently small, each tube in the restricted supremum lies in \(5Q\), in a slab \(c_n/4\le |s-t_0|\le2\) with a fixed sign of \(s-t_0\). Fix the height \(t_0\) and one sign. On this bounded slab and its image the map
\[
 (y',s)\longmapsto (Y',Y_n)=\left(y'/(s-t_0),\,1/(s-t_0)\right)
\]
and its inverse are uniformly Lipschitz, with Jacobian determinants bounded above and below. On the axis \(y'=x'+(s-t_0)v\) of any such tube the transformed line is \(Y'=v+Y_nx'\). Its direction is \((x',1)/|(x',1)|\) independently of \(v\). The image of the axis segment has bounded length and the image of the tube lies in its \(C_n\rho\)-neighborhood. Hence this image is covered by a bounded number of unit tubes of radius \(C_n\rho\) in that direction. The volumes of the original tube and of each covering tube are comparable to \(\rho^{n-1}\).

Transport \(|f|\) restricted to \(5Q\) and the fixed sign slab by the projective map and extend by zero. The resulting \(F\) depends on \(t_0\) and sign and works for all \(x'\) in the slice. Its \(L^n\) norm is \(\lesssim\|f\|_{L^n(5Q)}\) by the Jacobian bounds. Each original average is bounded by a constant times \(K_{C_n\rho}F((x',1)/|(x',1)|)\), using the measure comparison. The direction map is injective and has area Jacobian bounded below for the bounded \(x'\) in this cube. Apply the assumed Kakeya estimate to bound the slice \(L^n\) norm by \(C L(1/\rho)^{2A}\|f\|_{L^n(5Q)}\). Sum over the two signs and integrate in \(t_0\). Then translate over unit lattice cubes and use bounded overlap of their dilates \(5Q\). For \(\rho\) bounded below, the tubes lie in a fixed ball about \(x\) and have volume bounded below, so Young's inequality gives the asserted estimate directly.

\le C\delta^{-\sigma}\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}.

levels.title: Maximal estimate for a thin shell

levels.component_tex:
Write $s_+(p)=\max\{0,(n-1)/2-n/p\}$. For $2\le p<\infty$, choose $s_+(p)<\sigma<\alpha$. Choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty((1/2,2))$ with $\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\eta(2^jv)=1$ for $v>0$. Apply it to $v=1-\rho$ for $0\le\rho<1$. For $\delta=2^{-j}\le1/8$, the corresponding piece of $(1-\rho^2)_+^\alpha$ equals
\[
\delta^\alpha\psi_\delta((1-\rho)/\delta),\qquad
\psi_\delta(u)=\eta(u)u^\alpha(2-\delta u)^\alpha,
\]
with the expression defined as zero off the support of $\eta$. The profiles have uniform smooth seminorms. The remainder vanishes near $\rho=1$ and equals $(1-\rho^2)^\alpha$ near zero, so its radial extension is smooth and compactly supported. The kernel of this remainder has an integrable radial decreasing majorant. The supremum of its dilations is therefore bounded pointwise by a constant times the Hardy--Littlewood maximal function. Apply \ref{ms:lemma-10-2} to the remaining pieces. The sum of their maximal $L^p$ norms is bounded by
\[
C\sum_{j\ge3}2^{-j(\alpha-\sigma)}\|f\|_p.
\]
This proves the maximal bound on Schwartz functions, and gives the fixed-radius bound there since $\delta(p)=s_+(p)$ in this range.

Each fixed $B_r^\alpha$ is self-adjoint on Schwartz functions, and $\delta(p)=\delta(p')$ for conjugate exponents. Duality proves the fixed-radius bound for $1<p<2$. At $p=1,\infty$ the hypothesis is $\alpha>(n-1)/2$. Radial Fourier inversion gives the unit-radius kernel as a constant times $|x|^{-n/2-\alpha}J_{n/2+\alpha}(|x|)$, where $J_\nu$ is the Bessel function of the first kind. The kernel is bounded at zero and is $O(|x|^{-(n+1)/2-\alpha})$ at infinity, so its dilates $r^nK(rx)$ have a common $L^1$ norm. Density for finite $p$ and convolution at $p=\infty$ give the stated extensions.

For Schwartz functions with compact Fourier support, the symbols converge to one in all derivatives on the support as $r\to\infty$. The means then converge in the Schwartz topology. Density and the fixed-radius bound give norm convergence for $p<\infty$. For the almost everywhere and maximal claims, choose such $f_j$ with $\sum_j\|f-f_j\|_p<\infty$. The maximal bound on Schwartz functions implies that $\sum_j\sup_{r>0}|B_r^\alpha(f_{j+1}-f_j)|$ is finite almost everywhere. At every such point $B_r^\alpha f_j$ converges uniformly in $r>0$ to a continuous function of $r$, agreeing for each fixed $r$ almost everywhere with the bounded $L^p$ extension. Its supremum over $r$ is measurable by continuity, and Fatou's lemma gives the maximal estimate for $f$. Finally $f_j(x)\to f(x)$ almost everywhere, and uniform approximation in $r$ transfers convergence as $r\to\infty$ from $f_j$ to $f$.

levels.statement:
Let $n\ge 2$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and let $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ be arbitrary. For $r>0$ let $B_r^\alpha$ be the Fourier multiplier on $\mathbb R^n$ with symbol $(1-|\xi|^2/r^2)_+^\alpha$, and put
\[
\delta(p)=\max\{0,n|1/p-1/2|-1/2\}.
\]
If $\alpha>\delta(p)$, then
\[
\sup_{r>0}\|B_r^\alpha f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}
\le C_{n,p,\alpha}\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}.
\]
Under the same condition on $\alpha$, the means converge to $f$ in $L^p$ as $r\to\infty$ if $p<\infty$. If $2\le p<\infty$ and $\alpha>\max\{0,(n-1)/2-n/p\}$, then also
\[
\left\|\sup_{r>0}|B_r^\alpha f|\right\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}
\le C_{n,p,\alpha}\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)},
\]
and the means converge to $f$ almost everywhere as $r\to\infty$. The supremum is taken for a representative continuous in $r>0$ almost everywhere.

levels.component_tex:
For $r$ between $2^k$ and $2^{k+1}$ the symbol is supported in $2^{k-1}\le|\xi|\le2^{k+1}$. Choose a smooth annular symbol $\chi$ equal to one on $1/2\le|\xi|\le2$ and write $Q_k=\chi(2^{-k}D)$.

For $r=2^ks$, $1\le s\le2$, set $g_k(y)=(Q_k f)(2^{-k}y)$. Then $A_{\delta,r}f(2^{-k}y)=A_{\delta,s}g_k(y)$, and the factor $2^{-kn/p}$ in the output norm cancels $2^{kn/p}$ from $\|g_k\|_p$. Lemma~\ref{ms:shell-unit-radius} applies to $g_k$, which has Fourier support in the fixed annulus of $\chi$. The $L^p$ norm of the supremum in this octave is thus bounded by $C\delta^{-\sigma}\|Q_k f\|_p$. The supremum over the octaves is at most their pointwise $\ell^p$ norm. Since $p\ge2$, the Littlewood--Paley square-function inequality \cite{r-32}, Theorem~6.1.2, gives
\[
 \left(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\|Q_k f\|_p^p\right)^{1/p}
 \le\left\|\left(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|Q_k f|^2\right)^{1/2}\right\|_p
 \lesssim\|f\|_p.
\]

For $r$ between $2^k$ and $2^{k+1}$ the symbol is supported in $2^{k-1}\le|\xi|\le2^{k+1}$. Choose a smooth annular symbol $\chi$ equal to one on $1/2\le|\xi|\le2$ and write $Q_k=\chi(2^{-k}D)$.

For $r=2^ks$, $1\le s\le2$, set $g_k(y)=(Q_k f)(2^{-k}y)$. Then $A_{\delta,r}f(2^{-k}y)=A_{\delta,s}g_k(y)$, and the factor $2^{-kn/p}$ in the output norm cancels $2^{kn/p}$ from $\|g_k\|_p$. Lemma~\ref{ms:shell-unit-radius} applies to $g_k$, which has Fourier support in the fixed annulus of $\chi$. The $L^p$ norm of the supremum in this octave is thus bounded by $C\delta^{-\sigma}\|Q_k f\|_p$. The supremum over the octaves is at most their pointwise $\ell^p$ norm. Since $p\ge2$, the Littlewood--Paley square-function inequality \cite{r-32}, Theorem~6.1.2, gives
\[
 \left(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\|Q_k f\|_p^p\right)^{1/p}
 \le\left\|\left(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|Q_k f|^2\right)^{1/2}\right\|_p
 \lesssim\|f\|_p.
\]

levels.component_tex:
Set $U(t)=e^{-it|D|}$. With the scalar Fourier transform $\widehat\psi(t)=\int e^{-itu}\psi(u)\,du$, inversion gives
\[
 A_{\delta,r}g(x)=\frac{\delta r}{2\pi}
 \int_{\mathbb R}e^{itr}\widehat\psi(\delta rt)U(t)g(x)\,dt.
\]
The supremum for $1\le r\le2$ is bounded by $C_M\delta\int(1+\delta|t|)^{-M}|U(t)g(x)|\,dt$. On $R\le|t|\le2R$ with dyadic $R\ge1$, H\"older in time and \ref{ms:lemma-10-3} give an $L_x^p$ bound for the contribution of
\[

levels.component_tex: Put $g_R(x)=g(Rx)$. Its Fourier support is contained in $cR\le|\xi|\le CR$, and $U(t)g_R(x)=(U(Rt)g)(Rx)$. Apply \ref{ms:thm-1-1} on $1\le t\le2$ to $g_R$ at Sobolev order $\sigma$. The Sobolev multiplier $(1+|\xi|^2)^{\sigma/2}$ costs $O(R^\sigma)$ on this annulus: after insertion of a smooth annular cutoff and division by $R^\sigma$, its dilation to scale one has uniformly bounded derivatives of each fixed order. The change of variables contributes $R^{(n+1)/p}$ in the output and $\|g_R\|_p=R^{-n/p}\|g\|_p$, giving $R^{1/p+\sigma}$. Conjugation gives the negative-time bound. For $|t|\le1$, insert a fixed smooth annular cutoff equal to one on the support of $\widehat g$. The symbols of these cut-off propagators are uniformly smooth and compactly supported, so their kernels have bounded $L^1$ norms uniformly in $t$.

levels.component_tex:
The square-function argument needs a uniform $L^p$ bound for the sequence of smooth annular cutoffs supplied as inputs to the dilated operators.

\begin{Proposition}[Annular Littlewood--Paley bound]\label{ext:stein-annular-square}
Let $n\ge1$, $1<p<\infty$, and let $q\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ be supported in $\{c\le|\xi|\le C\}$ with $0<c\le C<\infty$. Use
\[
 \widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-ix\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx,\qquad
 \check q(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{ix\cdot\xi}q(\xi)\,d\xi .
\]
For $j\in\mathbb Z$, define $P_j=q(2^{-j}D)$ on Schwartz functions by
$\widehat{P_j f}(\xi)=q(2^{-j}\xi)\widehat f(\xi)$. On $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$ use the convolution formula $P_j f=2^{jn}\check q(2^j\cdot)*f$. Then
\[
 \left\|\left(\sum_{k\in F}|P_{k+\ell} f|^2\right)^{1/2}\right\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}
 \le C_{n,p,q}\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}
\]
for every finite $F\subset\mathbb Z$, every integer shift $\ell$, and every $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$. The bound also holds for the full sum. The undilated kernel $\check q$ is Schwartz and has integral zero because $q(0)=0$. Its decay and that of its first derivatives give the kernel bound in \cite{r-32}, Theorem~6.1.2, (6.1.3), so (6.1.4), p.~421, applies. Restriction to the indices $F+\ell$ preserves the bound.
\end{Proposition}

levels.title: Combining dilates

levels.component_tex:
For $p=2$, differentiate the symbol and use spatial Plancherel. Changing variables to $u=|\xi|^2/r^2$ in the inner integral gives
\[
\|\mathcal G_\alpha f\|_2^2=
2\alpha^2\int_0^1u(1-u)^{2\alpha-2}\,du\,\|f\|_2^2
=\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha-1}\|f\|_2^2.
\]
Suppose $p>2$. Set $s_+(p)=\max\{0,(n-1)/2-n/p\}$ and choose $\varepsilon>0$ so that $\sigma=s_+(p)+\varepsilon<\alpha-1/2$. On $r=2^k s$, $1\le s\le2$, put $\rho=2^{-k}|\xi|$ and use $dr/r=ds/s$, a measure comparable to $ds$. The multiplier of $r\partial_r B_r^\alpha$ is zero for $\rho>s$ and equals
\[
 m(s,\rho)=2\alpha \rho^2s^{-2\alpha}(s+\rho)^{\alpha-1}(s-\rho)^{\alpha-1}
 \qquad (\rho<s).
\]
This follows by differentiating the locally integrable positive-part power, which has no boundary delta term since $\alpha>0$.

Take a smooth cutoff equal to one near $\rho=s$ and supported where $|s-\rho|<1/2$ for $s\in[1,2]$. Insert a smooth cutoff in $s$ agreeing with one on $[1,2]$, with support in $(3/4,9/4)$. The factors preceding $(s-\rho)^{\alpha-1}$ times the cutoffs give a smooth compactly supported amplitude $A(s,\rho)$ with $\rho$ bounded away from zero. For $s-\rho>0$ split this boundary term using a smooth dyadic partition $\sum_j\eta(2^j(s-\rho))=1$ with $\eta\in C_c^\infty((1/2,2))$. The support leaves only $j\ge0$. With $\delta=2^{-j}$ and $\varphi(u)=\eta(u)u^{\alpha-1}$ on its support, each piece has symbol
\[
 \delta^{\alpha-1} A(s,\rho)\varphi((s-\rho)/\delta).
\]

For each $\delta$, let $T_\delta^{(k)}$ be the spatial dilation of the operator in \ref{ms:lemma-11-2}, with $s\in[1,2]$ unchanged. By integration by parts up to $N=n+3$ times in $\xi$ on a fixed compact annulus, its undilated kernel $K$ and first spatial derivatives have decay $C\delta^{-N}(1+|x|)^{-N}$ uniformly in $s$. In particular the same estimate holds for their norms in $H=L^2([1,2],ds)$ and $H^n$. Choose smooth annular projections $P_k$, dilates of one multiplier equal to one on the undilated frequency support. Apply \ref{ms:lemma-11-3} to the inputs $P_kf$, using the bounds in \ref{ms:lemma-11-2} for $B_p$ and $B_2$. Proposition~\ref{ext:stein-annular-square} bounds the input square norm by $C\|f\|_p$ for the chosen smooth annular projections. On all dyadic intervals of radii together the shell contributes at most
\[
 C\delta^{\alpha-1}
 \left(\delta^{1/2}+\delta+
 [1+\log(1/\delta)]^{1/2-1/p}\delta^{1/2-\sigma}\right)\|f\|_p.
\]
The sum over all $j$ converges since $\alpha-1/2-\sigma>0$.

The multiplier remaining away from the boundary is smooth, supported in $\rho\le2$ for $s\in[1,2]$, and vanishes to order two at zero. Split it by smooth annular cutoffs at $\rho\asymp2^\ell$, $\ell\le2$. Dividing each term by $2^{2\ell}$ and rescaling $\rho$ to the unit annulus gives symbols with uniformly bounded derivatives of every fixed order. The undilated kernels and their first derivatives then satisfy \ref{ms:lemma-11-3} at $\delta=1$ with uniform $C_*$. The same kernel decay and convolution bound give uniform $B_2$ and $B_p$. For each $\ell$ apply that lemma using the projections at scales $2^{k+\ell}$. Proposition~\ref{ext:stein-annular-square} with shift $\ell$ bounds their input square norm uniformly in $\ell$. The resulting bounds sum because $\sum_{\ell\le2}2^{2\ell}<\infty$.

These estimates apply initially to finite sets of $k$ and finite shell sums. levels.statement:
Let $n\ge2$, $2\le p<\infty$, and
\[
\alpha>\max\left\{\frac12,n\left(\frac12-\frac1p\right)\right\}.
\]
For $r>0$ let $B_r^\alpha$ be the Fourier multiplier with symbol $(1-|\xi|^2/r^2)_+^\alpha$. For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ define
\[
\mathcal G_\alpha f(x)
 =\left(\int_0^\infty |r\partial_r B_r^\alpha f(x)|^2\frac{dr}{r}\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Then $\|\mathcal G_\alpha f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le C_{n,p,\alpha}\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}$, and $\mathcal G_\alpha$ extends to $L^p(\mathbb R^n)$.

For $p=2$, differentiate the symbol and use spatial Plancherel. Changing variables to $u=|\xi|^2/r^2$ in the inner integral gives
\[
\|\mathcal G_\alpha f\|_2^2=
2\alpha^2\int_0^1u(1-u)^{2\alpha-2}\,du\,\|f\|_2^2
=\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha-1}\|f\|_2^2.
\]
Suppose $p>2$. Set $s_+(p)=\max\{0,(n-1)/2-n/p\}$ and choose $\varepsilon>0$ so that $\sigma=s_+(p)+\varepsilon<\alpha-1/2$. \[
 m(s,\rho)=2\alpha \rho^2s^{-2\alpha}(s+\rho)^{\alpha-1}(s-\rho)^{\alpha-1}
 \qquad (\rho<s).
\]
This follows by differentiating the locally integrable positive-part power, which has no boundary delta term since $\alpha>0$.

Take a smooth cutoff equal to one near $\rho=s$ and supported where $|s-\rho|<1/2$ for $s\in[1,2]$. Insert a smooth cutoff in $s$ agreeing with one on $[1,2]$, with support in $(3/4,9/4)$. The factors preceding $(s-\rho)^{\alpha-1}$ times the cutoffs give a smooth compactly supported amplitude $A(s,\rho)$ with $\rho$ bounded away from zero. For $s-\rho>0$ split this boundary term using a smooth dyadic partition $\sum_j\eta(2^j(s-\rho))=1$ with $\eta\in C_c^\infty((1/2,2))$. The support leaves only $j\ge0$. With $\delta=2^{-j}$ and $\varphi(u)=\eta(u)u^{\alpha-1}$ on its support, each piece has symbol
\[
 \delta^{\alpha-1} A(s,\rho)\varphi((s-\rho)/\delta).
\]

For each $\delta$, let $T_\delta^{(k)}$ be the spatial dilation of the operator in \ref{ms:lemma-11-2}, with $s\in[1,2]$ unchanged. By integration by parts up to $N=n+3$ times in $\xi$ on a fixed compact annulus, its undilated kernel $K$ and first spatial derivatives have decay $C\delta^{-N}(1+|x|)^{-N}$ uniformly in $s$. In particular the same estimate holds for their norms in $H=L^2([1,2],ds)$ and $H^n$. Apply \ref{ms:lemma-11-3} to the inputs $P_kf$, using the bounds in \ref{ms:lemma-11-2} for $B_p$ and $B_2$. \[

 \left(\delta^{1/2}+\delta+
 [1+\log(1/\delta)]^{1/2-1/p}\delta^{1/2-\sigma}\right)\|f\|_p.
\]
The sum over all $j$ converges since $\alpha-1/2-\sigma>0$.

The multiplier remaining away from the boundary is smooth, supported in $\rho\le2$ for $s\in[1,2]$, and vanishes to order two at zero. Split it by smooth annular cutoffs at $\rho\asymp2^\ell$, $\ell\le2$. Dividing each term by $2^{2\ell}$ and rescaling $\rho$ to the unit annulus gives symbols with uniformly bounded derivatives of every fixed order. The undilated kernels and their first derivatives then satisfy \ref{ms:lemma-11-3} at $\delta=1$ with uniform $C_*$. The same kernel decay and convolution bound give uniform $B_2$ and $B_p$. Let $U(t)=e^{-it|D|}$. Temporarily omit $A$, allow $s\in\mathbb R$, and denote the resulting operator by $V_\delta$. If $g$ is supported in a fixed compact annulus in frequency, the Fourier transform in $s$, taken with the phase $e^{-ist}$, gives $\delta\widehat\varphi(\delta t)U(t)g(x)$. Thus Plancherel in $s$ gives
\[
\|V_\delta g(x,\cdot)\|_{L_s^2}
=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\delta\|\widehat\varphi(\delta t)U(t)g(x)\|_{L_t^2}.
\]
On $R\le|t|\le2R$ with dyadic $R\ge1$, H\"older in time and \ref{ms:lemma-10-3} bound $\|U(t)g\|_{L_x^p L_t^2}$ on that interval by
$C R^{1/2-1/p}R^{1/p+\sigma}\|g\|_p$. For $|t|\le1$, use the short-time bound of \ref{ms:lemma-10-3} together with Minkowski's inequality since $p\ge2$. For any $b>1/2+\sigma$ these bounds give
\[
 \|V_\delta g\|_{L_x^p L_s^2(\mathbb R)}
 \lesssim \delta\left(1+\sum_{R=1,2,4,\ldots}
 R^{1/2+\sigma}(1+\delta R)^{-b}\right)\|g\|_p
 \lesssim \delta^{1/2-\sigma}\|g\|_p .
\]
The last inequality follows by splitting at $R=\delta^{-1}$.

To restore $A$, Fourier invert in its first argument. The symbols $\widehat A_1(\eta,|\xi|)$ are supported on a fixed compact annulus and have any fixed finite collection of derivatives bounded by $O_b((1+|\eta|)^{-b})$ for every $b>0$. The corresponding operators on $L^p$ have the same decay by the integrable kernel estimate for smooth compactly supported symbols. Integrate $e^{is\eta}V_\delta(\widehat A_1(\eta,|D|)f)$ in $d\eta/(2\pi)$, restricting to $s\in[1,2]$, and use Minkowski to obtain the first bound. For the second, spatial Plancherel suffices since for each frequency the bounded multiplier is supported on an $s$ interval of length $O(\delta)$.

Put $b_k=\|S^{(k)}f_k\|_H$, $h=(\sum_k b_k^2)^{1/2}$, and $W=(\sum_k |f_k|^2)^{1/2}$. Let $M$ be the Hardy--Littlewood maximal operator over cubes and set $L=\lceil(N+2)\log_2(2/\delta)\rceil$. For each dyadic cube $Q$ of side $2^{-j}$ and center $y$, compare $h$ with $c_Q=(\sum_{k\le j-L} b_k(y)^2)^{1/2}$. For $x,z\in Q$ and $k\le j-L$, the derivative bound and the mean value inequality give
\[
 \|S^{(k)}f_k(x)-S^{(k)}f_k(y)\|_H
 \lesssim C_*\delta^{-N}2^{k-j}MW(z).
\]
Indeed $2^k|x-z|\lesssim1$, and shifted kernels on the segment from $y$ to $x$ are dominated by $2^{nk}(1+2^k|z-\cdot|)^{-N}$ up to a fixed constant. Convolving this radial decreasing kernel with $W$ costs at most a constant times $MW(z)$. The square sum of the differences costs $CC_*\delta MW(z)$ since $\delta^{-N}2^{-L}\lesssim\delta$.

For $k\ge j+L$ split $f_k$ on $5Q$ and its complement, where $5Q$ is the concentric dilation of $Q$. Dilation preserves the $L^2$ operator norm, so for $z\in Q$,
\[
 \frac1{|Q|}\int_Q\sum_{k\ge j+L}
 \|S^{(k)}(f_k\mathbf1_{5Q})(x)\|_H^2\,dx
 \lesssim B_2^2 M(W^2)(z).
\]
For $x,z\in Q$, the kernel bound summed on successive doubles of $5Q$ gives
\[
 \|S^{(k)}(f_k\mathbf1_{(5Q)^c})(x)\|_H
 \lesssim C_*\delta^{-N}2^{-(N-n)(k-j)} MW(z).
\]
On a cube of side comparable to $2^{a-j}$, the distance from $x$ to the associated exterior shell is bounded below by a constant times $2^{a-j}$. The integral of $|f_k|$ over the cube is bounded by its volume times $MW(z)$, leaving a convergent sum in $a$ because $N>n$. The square sum over $k\ge j+L$ then costs $CC_*\delta MW(z)$.

For the fewer than $2L$ remaining $k$, H\"older in this finite set gives
\[
 \left(|Q|^{-1}\int_Q\sum_{|k-j|<L}b_k^2\right)^{1/2}
 \le(2L)^{1/2-1/p}F(z),\qquad
 F=\left(\sum_k[M(b_k^2)]^{p/2}\right)^{1/p}.
\]
As $p/2>1$, the scalar maximal theorem and invariance of $B_p$ under dilation yield
\[
 \|F\|_p^p\lesssim\sum_k\|b_k\|_p^p
 \le B_p^p\sum_k\|f_k\|_p^p\le B_p^p\|W\|_p^p.
\]
The triangle inequality for the Hilbert square norm and Cauchy--Schwarz on $Q$ now bound the mean of $|h-c_Q|$ by
\[
 C\left(C_*\delta MW(z)+B_2M(W^2)(z)^{1/2}
       +L^{1/2-1/p}F(z)\right).
\]
Replacing $c_Q$ by the mean $h_Q$ costs at most two. The dyadic sharp function $h^\#(z)=\sup_{Q\ni z}|Q|^{-1}\int_Q|h-h_Q|$, with the supremum over dyadic cubes, therefore has its $L^p$ norm bounded by the stated right-hand side, using the maximal theorem for $p$ and $p/2$. Apply the sharp function inequality $\|h\|_p\lesssim_p\|h^\#\|_p$ from \cite{r-74}, Chapter~IV, Section~3.6, Corollary~1. Its smaller-exponent hypothesis holds because
\[

 \le B_2^2\sum_k\|f_k\|_2^2<\infty
\]
and $2<p$.

levels.statement:
Let $d\geq 1$, $p_c=2(d+1)/d$, and $B_d=B(0,1)\subset\mathbb R^d$. For $g$ on $B_d$ set
\[
Eg(x,t)=\int_{B_d}e^{\mathrm i(x\cdot v+t|v|^2)}g(v)\,\mathrm dv.
\]
If $1<a\leq\infty$, $p_c<b<\infty$, and $b>(d+2)a'/d$, where $1/a+1/a'=1$, then
\[
\|Eg\|_{L^b(\mathbb R^{d+1})}\lesssim_{d,a,b}\|g\|_{L^a(B_d)}.
\]

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a compact interval, and let $S(t)=e^{\mathrm i t\Delta}$ denote the Fourier multiplier $e^{-\mathrm i t|\xi|^2}$ on $\mathbb R^d$. If $N\geq 2$ and $f$ is Schwartz with $\operatorname{supp}\widehat f\subset B(0,N)$, then
\[
\|S(t)f\|_{L^{p_c}(\mathbb R^d\times I)}
 \lesssim_{d,I}[\log(2+N)]^{2/p_c}\|f\|_{L^{p_c}(\mathbb R^d)}.
\]

If $p_c<p<\infty$ and $p\leq r\leq\infty$, set $s=d(1-2/p)-2/r$, with $1/\infty=0$. For every Schwartz $f$,
\[
\|S(t)f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d;L^r(I))}
 \lesssim_{d,p,r,I}\|f\|_{B^s_{p,p}(\mathbb R^d)}
 \lesssim_{d,p,s}\|(1-\Delta)^{s/2}f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}.
\]

levels.component_tex:
The local extension bound of \ref{ms:lemma-12-cap} is $O_\varepsilon(R^\varepsilon)$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. The same holds on a fixed larger parameter ball. In fact, changing from $v$ to $Lv$ for fixed $L>1$ changes the physical coordinates by $(x,t)\mapsto (Lx,L^2t)$ and dilates the radius by at most a fixed factor. A smooth cutoff on that larger patch equal to one on $B_d$, times parameter measure $\mathrm dv$, gives a compactly supported smooth surface density $\mu$ with
\[
|\widehat\mu(x,t)|\lesssim (1+|(x,t)|)^{-d/2}.
\]
For $|x|$ much larger than $|t|$, this follows by integration by parts. Otherwise, when $|(x,t)|$ is large, the Hessian of the phase in $v$ is $2t I_d$ with $|t|\gtrsim |(x,t)|$, and stationary phase gives the bound.

By duality the local estimate gives
\[
\|\widehat F(v,|v|^2)\|_{L^{p_c'}(\mu)}
 \lesssim_\varepsilon R^\varepsilon\|F\|_{L^{p_c'}(\mathbb R^{d+1})}
\]
for smooth $F$ supported in any ball of radius $R\geq1$. To see that the cutoff does not change the local assumption, extend against $\mu$ by applying the enlarged-patch extension to the product of the input and the cutoff. The cutoff is bounded, so the $L^{p_c}(\mu)$ norm bounds the corresponding $L^{p_c}(\mathrm dv)$ norm of the product. Apply Tao's epsilon-removal theorem \cite{r-75}, Theorem~1.2, in the compact hypersurface form of Kim \cite{r-46}, Theorem~5.3. For a compact smooth hypersurface measure with power Fourier decay, local restriction at $1<u\leq v\leq 2$ with an arbitrarily small power loss on every ball implies global restriction from $L^w$ to $L^v(\mu)$ for $1\leq w<u$. Here $u=v=p_c'\in(1,2)$. Duality and zero extension of densities from $B_d$ therefore give $E:L^{p_c}(B_d)\to L^q(\mathbb R^{d+1})$ for every $p_c<q<\infty$. The finite measure of $B_d$ gives $E:L^q\to L^q$ in this range.

If $a\geq b$, use $q=b$ and the finite measure of $B_d$. If $a<b$, set $q=1+b/a'$. The assumption gives $q>1+(d+2)/d=p_c$, and $a<b$ gives $q<b$. Interpolate $E:L^1\to L^\infty$ and $E:L^q\to L^q$ at $\theta=q/b$. Then $1/b=\theta/q$ and $1/a=1-\theta+\theta/q$. This is the interpolation calculation used in \ref{ms:cor-9-3} for the sphere.

levels.component_tex:
Apply the local spherical extension estimate \ref{ms:lemma-9-2} with $n=d+1$. Its logarithmic exponent is $A=2/p_c$ by the critical annular bound \ref{ms:thm-1-2}. For $0<\delta\leq 1/2$, parametrize a cap on $S^d$ by $\omega(v)=(\delta v,\sqrt{1-\delta^2|v|^2})$, $v\in B_d$. Define the spherical density $G$ there by $G(\omega(v))=g(v)\sqrt{1-\delta^2|v|^2}$ and set it to zero off the cap. Then
\[
G(\omega)\,\mathrm d\sigma(\omega)=\delta^d g(v)\,\mathrm dv,
\qquad
\|G\|_{L^{p_c}(S^d)}\lesssim \delta^{d/p_c}\|g\|_{p_c}.
\]
At $X=(x/\delta,-2t/\delta^2)$ its spherical extension is $\delta^d e^{-2\mathrm it/\delta^2} E_\delta g(x,t)$, where $E_\delta$ is the extension with $|v|^2$ replaced by
\[
q_\delta(v)=\frac{2(1-\sqrt{1-\delta^2|v|^2})}{\delta^2}.
\]
The change to $X$ has absolute Jacobian $2\delta^{-(d+2)}$, and maps $B(0,R)$ into $B(0,CR/\delta^2)$. The spherical bound therefore gives
\[
\|E_\delta g\|_{L^{p_c}(B(0,R))}
 \lesssim \delta^{-d+(d+2)/p_c+d/p_c}
 [\log(2+R/\delta^2)]^A\|g\|_{p_c}.
\]
The exponent of $\delta$ vanishes. Uniformly on $B_d$, $q_\delta(v)=|v|^2+O(\delta^2)$. Since $|t|\leq R$ on the observation ball, the pointwise difference is bounded by $CR\delta^2\|g\|_1$. Its $L^{p_c}$ norm there is bounded by $C R^{1+(d+1)/p_c}\delta^2\|g\|_{p_c}$. With $\delta=(2R)^{-(d+2)}$ this is $O(\|g\|_{p_c})$ and $\log(2+R/\delta^2)\lesssim_d \log(2+R)$. For a ball centered at $z=(z_x,z_t)$ apply the estimate at the origin to $e^{\mathrm i(z_x\cdot v+z_t|v|^2)}g(v)$.

levels.component_tex:
Write $p=p_c$, $A=2/p_c$, $S(t)=e^{\mathrm it\Delta}$, and $I_0=[1/2,1]$. Fix $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B(0,2))$ equal to one on $B(0,1)$, and write $P_N=\chi(D/N)$, so that $P_Nf=f$. Tile $\mathbb R^d$ by cubes $Q$ of side $N$ and let $30Q$ be the concentric cube of side $30N$.

For $|z|\geq8N$ and $t\in I_0$, the kernel $K_{N,t}$ of $S(t)P_N$ satisfies
\[
|K_{N,t}(z)|\leq C_M N^d(1+N|z|)^{-M}.
\]
Indeed, after $\xi=N\eta$ the phase gradient in $\eta$ is $Nz-2tN^2\eta$, of magnitude at least $N|z|/2$ on the cutoff support. Its derivatives of positive order are either $O(N^2)$ or zero, and $N^2\lesssim N|z|$. Iterated integration by parts gives the uniform bound. For $x\in Q$ and $y\notin30Q$ we have $|x-y|\geq8N$, so the far contribution on every cube is bounded by the same convolution of $|f|$ with $C_M N^d(1+N|\cdot|)^{-M}$. For $M>d$ the latter kernel has bounded $L^1$ norm, giving a bound $O(\|f\|_p)$ on $\mathbb R^d\times I_0$ by Young's inequality.

For the near contribution translate $Q$ to the origin and put $h=f\mathbf 1_{30Q}$ in the translated coordinates. The two multipliers commute on $L^2$, and
\[
S(t)P_Nh(x)=P_NS(t)h(x)
 =\int\check\chi(w)\,S(t)h(x-w/N)\,\mathrm dw.
\]
Here $\check\chi$ is the inverse Fourier transform with the factor $(2\pi)^{-d}$. Take $\lambda=16\sqrt d\,N$ and $g(v)=h(\lambda v)$, which is supported in $B_d=B(0,1)\subset\mathbb R^d$. Since $h\in L^1\cap L^2$, the Fresnel formula applies and its spatial integral is absolutely convergent. Making the substitution $y=\lambda v$ yields
\[
|S(t)h(z)|=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\lambda^d
 \left|Eg\!\left(-\frac{\lambda z}{2t},\frac{\lambda^2}{4t}\right)\right|,
\quad
Eg(x,t)=\int_{B_d}e^{\mathrm i(x\cdot v+t|v|^2)}g(v)\,\mathrm dv.
\]
For $z=x-w/N$ with $x\in Q$ and $t\in I_0$, the two arguments lie together in a ball of radius $C_d(N^2+|w|)$. The map $(x,t)\mapsto(-\lambda(x-w/N)/(2t),\lambda^2/(4t))$ is one-to-one by its last coordinate. Its absolute Jacobian is $(\lambda/(2t))^d\lambda^2/(4t^2)\asymp_d\lambda^{d+2}$. Since $\|g\|_p=\lambda^{-d/p}\|h\|_p$, \ref{ms:lemma-12-cap} gives
\[
\|S(t)h(x-w/N)\|_{L^p(Q\times I_0)}
 \lesssim_d \lambda^{d-(2d+2)/p}[\log(2+N^2+|w|)]^A\|h\|_p.
\]
The power of $\lambda$ is zero. By Minkowski's inequality and the rapid decay of $\check\chi$, the near contribution has norm at most $C[\log(2+N)]^A\|f\|_{L^p(30Q)}$. Sum its $p$th powers over $Q$ using the bounded overlap of $30Q$, and add the far bound. This proves the claim on $I_0$.

On $[a/2,a]$, $a>0$, set $f_a(x)=f(\sqrt a\,x)$. Then $S(t)f_a(x)=(S(at)f)(\sqrt a\,x)$ and the support radius for $\widehat f_a$ is at most $\sqrt a\,N$. Scaling the estimate on $I_0$, the spatial factors cancel and leave
\[
\|S(t)f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d\times[a/2,a])}
 \lesssim_d a^{1/p}[\log(2+\max(2,\sqrt a\,N))]^A\|f\|_p.
\]
For bounded positive times sum the $p$th powers over intervals with $a=T2^{-j}$, $j\geq0$, and fixed $T>0$. The logarithm is bounded by $C_T\log(2+N)$, and $\sum_j T2^{-j}<\infty$. For negative times use $S(-t)f=\overline{S(t)\overline f}$, with the same frequency-ball condition. This gives the result on $I$.

\]
The power of $\lambda$ is zero. By Minkowski's inequality and the rapid decay of $\check\chi$, the near contribution has norm at most $C[\log(2+N)]^A\|f\|_{L^p(30Q)}$. Sum its $p$th powers over $Q$ using the bounded overlap of $30Q$, and add the far bound. This proves the claim on $I_0$.

On $[a/2,a]$, $a>0$, set $f_a(x)=f(\sqrt a\,x)$. Then $S(t)f_a(x)=(S(at)f)(\sqrt a\,x)$ and the support radius for $\widehat f_a$ is at most $\sqrt a\,N$. Scaling the estimate on $I_0$, the spatial factors cancel and leave
\[
\|S(t)f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d\times[a/2,a])}
 \lesssim_d a^{1/p}[\log(2+\max(2,\sqrt a\,N))]^A\|f\|_p.
\]
For bounded positive times sum the $p$th powers over intervals with $a=T2^{-j}$, $j\geq0$, and fixed $T>0$. The logarithm is bounded by $C_T\log(2+N)$, and $\sum_j T2^{-j}<\infty$. For negative times use $S(-t)f=\overline{S(t)\overline f}$, with the same frequency-ball condition. This gives the result on $I$.
